text:
Connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) are widely expected to transform personal mobility. Automation promises large safety gains by removing human error, which contributes to the vast majority of crashes [1]. It also promises energy savings through smoother driving, platooning, eco-routing, and right-sizing of vehicles [2,3]. Perhaps most distinctively, CAVs would free occupants from the task of driving, allowing travel time to be spent working, resting, or at leisure, and so reducing the perceived cost of time spent in a vehicle [4,5]. Taken together, these features suggest that CAVs could make driving substantially cheaper in both fuel and time terms.

Whether this translates into lower energy consumption and emissions is far from certain. Engineering studies of CAV technologies typically estimate energy use per mile under fixed travel demand, and some find reductions of 10-30% or more for individual vehicles [2,6]. Yet travel demand is not fixed. Basic economic theory predicts that when the price of a good falls, consumption of it rises. In transportation, lower fuel cost per mile increases vehicle miles traveled (VMT), offsetting part of the energy savings. This is the direct rebound effect, which has been studied extensively in the context of fuel economy standards [7,8]. If the increase in travel is large enough to exceed the efficiency gain, net energy use rises, a case known as backfire. CAVs complicate this picture because they act on a second price: the time cost of travel. Because time is a binding constraint on household activity, and travel time is valued at a substantial fraction of the wage [9,10], reductions in its burden could induce much larger increases in travel than fuel savings alone [11,12].

Several studies have sought to forecast the system-level effects of CAVs, using travel demand models, simulations, and scenario analyses [5,11,13]. Their projections range widely, from sizable energy reductions to more than a doubling of energy use, depending largely on assumptions about how travelers respond to changes in the cost of travel. Wadud et al. [11], for example, show that outcomes hinge on the interaction of efficiency gains, the value of travel time, and induced demand. Despite the importance of these behavioral parameters, the empirical basis for them is thin. Most existing elasticity estimates describe responses to fuel price or fuel cost per mile, and are often drawn from aggregate time series or from earlier decades when travel patterns and incomes differed [7,8,14]. Estimates of responsiveness to time cost are scarcer still, and typically come from stated preference or congestion pricing contexts that may not generalize to the household-level decision about how much to drive [10,15]. As a result, forecasts of CAV-induced travel often rely on assumed rather than measured elasticities.

This paper addresses that gap by estimating elasticities of VMT demand with respect to both fuel and time costs using recent household-level data, and by applying them to simulate the consequences of full, private CAV adoption. We begin by developing a microeconomic model of household VMT choice under both income and time constraints. In this framework, a household allocates scarce money and time among travel and other goods, and the full price of a mile of travel includes both the fuel cost and the monetized value of the time spent traveling. The model yields a demand function for VMT in which the elasticities with respect to fuel cost and time cost are separately identified, and it clarifies how the two should relate to household income and the wage. We then estimate the model using the 2017 United States National Household Travel Survey (NHTS), which provides detailed data on household vehicles, fuel economy, travel, and socioeconomic characteristics. Fuel cost per mile is constructed from vehicle fuel economy and fuel prices, while time cost is predicted from wage information, allowing us to exploit cross-sectional variation in both.

Our analysis yields three main findings. First, the central estimate of the combined price elasticity of VMT demand is -0.4, which differs substantially from many earlier estimates that are smaller in magnitude. Second, demand appears more elastic among wealthier households, suggesting that the travel response to CAVs will be unevenly distributed across the income distribution. Third, households at all income levels are more sensitive to time costs than to fuel costs, implying that the time-saving feature of CAVs may matter more for induced travel than their fuel-saving feature.

Using these estimates, we simulate VMT and energy outcomes under a range of plausible changes in the fuel and time costs of travel brought about by full private CAV adoption. We forecast an increase in travel demand of 2-47% for an average household, with the wide range reflecting genuine uncertainty about how much CAVs will reduce the time burden and improve efficiency. In the more extreme scenarios, particularly for higher income groups, induced travel is large enough to produce backfire. This outcome poses a considerable challenge to policy goals concerning not only energy use and greenhouse gas emissions, but also congestion and local air pollution.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related literature. Section 3 presents the theoretical model and the empirical strategy. Section 4 describes the data. Section 5 reports the elasticity estimates, and Section 6 presents the simulation of CAV impacts. Section 7 discusses policy implications and concludes.

We model household vehicle miles traveled (VMT) as the outcome of utility maximization under both income and time constraints, following the household production tradition of Becker [1] and DeSerpa [2]. Household i derives utility U(x, m, v) from a composite good x, leisure and other non-travel time, and VMT v. The household faces a budget constraint, x + p_f v = w·t_w + y, where p_f is the fuel cost per mile, w is the wage rate, t_w is hours worked, and y is non-labor income. It also faces a time constraint, t_w + t_l + τv = T, where τ is travel time per mile, t_l is leisure time, and T is total available time. Combining the two constraints yields a full-income constraint in which the effective price of a mile is the generalized cost p_g = p_f + wτ. Fuel cost and time cost therefore enter demand as additive components of a single price, and the household's VMT demand is v = v(p_f, wτ, Y), where Y is full income wT + y.

**Elasticity specification.** We specify a log-linear demand function:

ln v_i = α + β_f ln p_{f,i} + β_t ln(c_{t,i}) + γ'Z_i + ε_i,

where c_t is the time cost per mile (the product of the value of travel time and the inverse of average speed), Z is a vector of household covariates, and β_f and β_t are the elasticities of VMT with respect to fuel and time costs. The combined price elasticity is the sum β_f + β_t, which gives the response to a proportional change in both cost components. We also estimate specifications with interaction terms between the cost variables and income bracket indicators to test for heterogeneity in elasticities across the income distribution [3].

**Data.** Fuel cost and travel data come from the 2017 United States National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) [4]. The NHTS records household demographics, vehicle attributes, and travel diaries, with odometer-based annual VMT estimates for each vehicle. We restrict the sample to households that own at least one vehicle and report valid income, vehicle, and location information. We drop observations with implausible VMT or fuel economy values. Fuel cost per mile is computed as the regional gasoline price divided by the vehicle's fuel economy. Fuel prices come from state-level or Census division-level monthly averages published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration [5], and fuel economy comes from the EPA ratings matched to each vehicle's make, model, and year [6]. Household-level VMT and fuel cost are the VMT-weighted aggregates across vehicles. All estimates apply NHTS household weights.

**Time cost.** Travel time cost is not directly observed, so we predict it from wages. The NHTS reports income and employment but not hourly wages. We therefore impute wages using a Mincer-type regression [7] fitted to the Current Population Survey [8], with education, age, occupation, and region as predictors, and apply it to NHTS respondents. The value of travel time is set to a fraction of the predicted wage. Our central case uses 50%, consistent with the empirical literature on the value of travel time savings, which typically finds values between 35% and 60% of the wage rate [9,10]. We test alternative fractions of 25% and 100% as sensitivity checks. Travel time per mile is derived from reported trip durations and distances.

**Identification.** The main identification concern is endogeneity of the cost variables. Households choosing longer commutes may choose more efficient vehicles, producing correlation between fuel cost per mile and the error term [11]. To address this, we instrument fuel cost per mile with regional gasoline prices and the vehicle's fuel economy rating, and we control for the type of vehicle choice using vehicle class. We further instrument time cost with metropolitan-area measures of population density and the predicted wage based only on demographic and occupational characteristics. We check instrument strength using first-stage F-statistics and report overidentification tests. We compare the IV estimates against OLS and against fixed-effect specifications that absorb Census division effects. Standard errors are clustered at the state level.

**Simulation of CAV scenarios.** We use the estimated elasticities to simulate the impact of full private adoption of CAVs. CAV effects are expressed as proportional changes to the two cost components. Fuel cost per mile falls through improvements in efficiency from platooning, eco-driving, and right-sizing, with changes ranging from 0% to −30% based on prior engineering analyses [12,13]. Time cost per mile falls as occupants shift time to productive or leisure activities, with reductions from 0% to −80% of the baseline value of time [14]. We evaluate a grid of fuel and time cost scenarios, with low, central, and high cases. For each household, the predicted VMT change is

ΔlnV = β_f Δln p_f + β_t Δln c_t,

using the exact exponentiated form for large changes. We report the aggregate and income-group-specific changes in VMT, with confidence intervals obtained by bootstrapping the estimation and simulation steps with 1,000 replications.

**Energy rebound and backfire.** Direct rebound is defined as the fraction of the engineering energy savings offset by induced travel [15]. For a fuel economy improvement that reduces energy use per mile by fraction e, with VMT changing by factor (1 + ΔV), net energy use changes by (1 − e)(1 + ΔV) − 1. Backfire occurs when this quantity is positive, that is, when induced VMT exceeds the efficiency gain. We compute net energy changes for each scenario and income group, and we identify the combinations of fuel and time cost reductions that produce backfire.

**Robustness.** We test alternative functional forms, including a translog specification, alternative value-of-time fractions, exclusion of multi-vehicle households, and urban-only subsamples. We also compare our elasticities with those of earlier work based on fuel cost alone [16,17] to explain differences from prior estimates.

We estimated the VMT demand model using 2017 NHTS household records, with fuel cost per mile computed from reported vehicle fuel economy and regional gasoline prices, and time cost per mile derived from wage-based valuations of travel time and observed average speeds. Results are reported first for the elasticity estimates, then for heterogeneity by income, and finally for the CAV adoption simulations.

**Elasticity estimates**

Our central estimate of the combined price elasticity of VMT demand, defined as the sum of the elasticities with respect to fuel cost per mile and time cost per mile, is -0.4 (95% confidence interval: -0.47 to -0.33). This is substantially larger in magnitude than the fuel-cost-only elasticities commonly reported in the rebound literature, which typically fall between -0.05 and -0.2 [1,2]. Decomposing the combined estimate, the elasticity of VMT with respect to fuel cost per mile is -0.09 (SE 0.02), whereas the elasticity with respect to time cost per mile is -0.31 (SE 0.04). The difference between the two coefficients is statistically significant (p < 0.01), indicating that households respond roughly three times as strongly to changes in time cost as to equivalent proportional changes in fuel cost.

Results were robust to several alternative specifications. Including state fixed effects and controls for household size, number of vehicles, number of workers, urban form, and vehicle type changed the combined elasticity by less than 0.05. Instrumenting fuel economy with vehicle model-year characteristics to address self-selection of efficient vehicles by households with differing travel needs produced a slightly smaller fuel-cost elasticity (-0.07) and a similar time-cost elasticity. Using alternative values of travel time, from 35% to 100% of the hourly wage, shifted the time-cost elasticity between -0.22 and -0.38 but left the qualitative ranking of the two elasticities unchanged. Excluding households with extreme VMT values (top and bottom 1%) yielded estimates within one standard error of the baseline.

**Heterogeneity by income**

Demand elasticity varied systematically with household income. For households in the lowest income tercile, the combined elasticity was -0.28 (SE 0.05), rising in magnitude to -0.41 in the middle tercile and -0.52 in the highest tercile. A test of equality across the lowest and highest terciles rejected the null at the 5% level. Thus, wealthier households exhibit more elastic VMT demand, consistent with a greater discretionary component of their travel and a weaker income constraint. At all income levels, the time-cost elasticity exceeded the fuel-cost elasticity in magnitude. The ratio was smallest in the lowest tercile (approximately 2:1) and largest in the highest tercile (approximately 4:1), reflecting the larger wage-derived time costs faced by high-income households and the diminishing budget share of fuel.

**Simulated effects of full private CAV adoption**

We used the estimated elasticities to simulate changes in household VMT and energy use under full private CAV adoption. Because the magnitudes of CAV effects on fuel economy and travel time cost remain uncertain, we considered a range of scenarios. Fuel cost per mile was assumed to fall by 0% to 30%, reflecting efficiency gains from platooning, smoother driving, and optimized routing [3,4]. Time cost per mile was assumed to fall by 0% to 60%, reflecting the ability to use in-vehicle time for work or leisure, with the upper bound representing near-complete conversion of travel time to productive or enjoyable use [5].

Across this range, the simulated increase in VMT for an average household is 2% to 47%. In the low scenario (a 10% reduction in fuel cost and a 5% reduction in time cost), VMT rises by approximately 2.5%. In the intermediate scenario (a 20% fuel cost reduction and a 30% time cost reduction), VMT rises by roughly 13%. In the high scenario (a 30% fuel cost reduction and a 60% time cost reduction), VMT rises by 47%, a figure that reflects the nonlinearity of the constant-elasticity demand function at large price changes. Time cost reductions account for the majority of induced travel in all but the lowest scenarios; in the intermediate scenario, approximately 85% of the VMT increase is attributable to the time cost channel.

Energy use changes depend on the net of induced VMT and the per-mile efficiency gain. In the low and intermediate scenarios, energy use falls for the average household, by 6.8% and 7.5% respectively, implying rebound effects well above those typically attributed to fuel economy alone, since the induced travel offsets a large share of the efficiency gain. In the high scenario, VMT growth of 47% exceeds the 30% reduction in energy per mile, yielding a net increase in household energy use of approximately 3%, that is, backfire.

Backfire was more likely among higher-income households. In the top income tercile, energy use rose in scenarios where fuel cost reductions were 20% or greater and time cost reductions exceeded roughly 45%, while in the lowest tercile net energy use remained below baseline in all but the most extreme combinations. Under the high scenario, simulated VMT increases were approximately 31%, 46%, and 62% for the lowest, middle, and highest terciles, respectively, with corresponding energy changes of -10%, +2%, and +14%.

Sensitivity analyses indicated that the results depend primarily on the assumed time cost reduction. Varying the time-cost elasticity across its 95% confidence interval changed the intermediate-scenario VMT increase from 9% to 18%. Varying the fuel-cost elasticity across its interval changed the result by less than 2 percentage points. Together, these results suggest that the energy outcome of CAV adoption is governed chiefly by how strongly automation reduces the perceived cost of time in the vehicle rather than by its efficiency benefits.

Our results suggest that the introduction of private CAVs could substantially increase household travel demand, and that the energy consequences depend on the balance between efficiency gains and induced travel. The central combined price elasticity of VMT demand of -0.4 is larger in magnitude than the fuel-cost elasticities typically reported in the rebound literature, which are often between -0.05 and -0.3 [1,2]. Two features of our approach likely explain this difference. First, we model the full generalized cost of travel, including time, so the combined elasticity reflects responses to both money and time prices rather than to fuel cost alone. Second, our cross-sectional identification uses variation in fuel cost per mile across households in the 2017 NHTS, which may capture longer-run adjustments in vehicle choice and residential location that short-run panel estimates miss. Because the estimates draw on cross-sectional variation, they may also be affected by unobserved heterogeneity, and we interpret them as medium- to long-run responses rather than as causal effects of a sudden price change.

Two heterogeneity findings deserve emphasis. Wealthier households appear to have more elastic demand, contrary to the common expectation that higher income reduces price sensitivity. One explanation is that higher-income households have more discretionary travel and more flexibility to substitute trips, destinations, and modes, while lower-income households' travel is dominated by inelastic commuting and essential trips. Another is that high-income households own more vehicles, so marginal trips are easier to add. Moreover, households at all income levels respond more strongly to time cost than to fuel cost. This is consistent with evidence that travelers value time savings highly relative to out-of-pocket costs [3,4], and it implies that CAV effects on the time burden of driving, through the ability to work, rest, or play en route, may matter more for travel demand than any efficiency gains in fuel cost. Because our time-cost measure is derived from wages, it is an imperfect proxy for the actual valuation of time, particularly for households with nonwage income, retirees, or variable work hours, and measurement error could attenuate or distort the estimated time elasticity.

The simulations indicate that full private CAV adoption could raise average household VMT by roughly 2% to 47%, depending on how much CAVs reduce the time and fuel costs of travel. The wide range reflects genuine uncertainty about technology and deployment: the degree to which travel time is made productive or less onerous, the extent of platooning and eco-driving gains, and the degree of electrification. At the lower end of the range, efficiency gains would probably dominate and net energy use would fall. At the upper end, induced travel can offset or exceed per-mile energy savings, producing backfire, especially among higher-income households whose demand is most elastic and whose time costs fall most in absolute terms. This is consistent with earlier scenario analyses showing that the energy effects of automation could range from large reductions to large increases [5,6]. Our contribution is to ground the behavioral component of such scenarios in observed household travel responses.

These findings have several policy implications. Improvements in vehicle efficiency alone may not be sufficient to reduce energy use and emissions once CAVs lower the time cost of driving. Policymakers may need to pair automation with measures that manage demand, such as road or congestion pricing, VMT-based charges, parking policy, and incentives for shared and pooled rides. Because backfire is more likely among wealthier households, pricing instruments could be targeted or designed with revenue recycling to limit regressive impacts. Decarbonizing the energy supply and promoting electrified CAVs would reduce the environmental consequences of any induced travel, but would not remove its effects on congestion, land use, and safety exposure. Induced VMT also bears on local air pollution and infrastructure costs, which suggests that the benefits of CAV technologies will be realized only if travel growth is anticipated in planning.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The elasticities are estimated from conventional vehicle users and are extrapolated to a technology that will alter the travel experience in ways not observed in current data. Elasticities might change at large reductions in time cost, so the constant-elasticity extrapolation may overstate or understate responses at the upper end of our scenarios. We consider only private ownership with full adoption; shared automated fleets, empty repositioning trips, new user groups such as older adults and people with disabilities, and changes in vehicle ownership and residential location could all alter the net effect [7]. We also do not model congestion feedback, in which induced travel slows traffic and partially counteracts further demand growth, nor do we model changes in vehicle size, power, and amenities that could offset efficiency gains. Finally, the NHTS is a single cross-section, and self-reported data and imputed fuel costs introduce measurement error.

Future research should combine revealed-preference data with stated-preference experiments or pilot deployments of automated vehicles to test whether time-cost responses extrapolate, and should integrate our demand elasticities into network and lifecycle energy models. Panel data and quasi-experimental variation would help separate causal price effects from selection.

In conclusion, we developed a microeconomic model of VMT choice under income and time constraints and estimated a central combined price elasticity of demand of -0.4, with greater sensitivity to time than fuel costs and greater elasticity among wealthier households. Applying these estimates, we find that full private CAV adoption could increase household travel by 2-47%, and that energy backfire is plausible, particularly for higher-income groups. Realizing the energy and environmental promise of CAVs will therefore require policies that address travel demand as well as vehicle efficiency.

Random coefficients models are a central tool in empirical economics. They allow for unobserved heterogeneity in consumer preferences and thereby yield flexible substitution patterns that are not available in the standard multinomial logit model. Their applications span industrial organization, transportation, health, and environmental economics [1, 2, 3]. In the most common specification, a decision maker chooses among alternatives based on a linear index of observed characteristics whose coefficients vary across individuals according to an unknown distribution. The object of interest is this mixing distribution, since it determines own- and cross-price elasticities, welfare effects, and counterfactual market shares.

The usual practice is to impose a parametric family on the mixing distribution, typically a multivariate normal, and to estimate its parameters by maximum likelihood or simulated methods [2, 4]. Such assumptions are convenient but restrictive. Misspecification can produce misleading policy conclusions, and parametric forms rule out features such as multimodality, skewness, or discrete types that may be present in the population. This has motivated a literature on nonparametric identification and estimation of the mixing distribution [5, 6, 7]. Nonparametric estimation is nevertheless challenging: the problem is an ill-posed inverse problem, and many estimators are computationally demanding, particularly when the coefficient vector is high dimensional.

Fox, Kim, Ryan, and Bajari [8] proposed an appealing approach to this difficulty. They fix a grid of coefficient vectors and treat the mixing distribution as a vector of unknown weights on the grid points. Because choice probabilities are linear in these weights, the weights can be estimated by constrained least squares, requiring them to be nonnegative and to sum to one. The resulting estimator solves a convex quadratic program, avoids nonlinear optimization over the distribution's parameters, and is easy to implement. It has been used in a variety of applications [9, 10, 11], and its consistency has been established under general conditions [8]. A feature noted repeatedly in practice is that the estimated distribution is sparse: only a small number of grid points receive positive weight, so the estimate is a discrete distribution with few support points. This is often at odds with the smooth distributions that researchers expect and can make the estimated heterogeneity look artificially coarse.

This paper explains this sparsity and uses the explanation to improve the estimator. Our first contribution is to show that the estimator of Fox et al. is a special case of the nonnegative LASSO [12, 13]. The adding-up constraint on the weights, combined with nonnegativity, makes the sum of the weights constant, so that the LASSO penalty, the sum of absolute values of the weights, is implicitly active at a fixed level. The well-known selection property of the \(\ell_1\) penalty [12, 14] then accounts for the sparse solutions found in applications. Moreover, the link allows us to draw on a rich body of results on the LASSO, including conditions for support recovery and prediction error bounds [15, 16, 17].

Our second contribution is a generalization. Since the original estimator is a nonnegative LASSO, it is natural to add a ridge-type \(\ell_2\) penalty, which turns it into a nonnegative elastic net [18]. The elastic net is known to behave better than the LASSO when regressors are highly correlated, since it tends to select groups of correlated variables rather than arbitrarily choosing one among them [18, 19]. This situation is exactly what arises in the random coefficients setting, where grid points close to each other generate nearly collinear columns of choice probabilities. The proposed estimator therefore spreads weight over neighboring grid points and yields less sparse, more stable estimates. Because the original estimator corresponds to a zero value of the additional penalty parameter, our estimator nests it. When the penalty parameter is chosen, for example by cross-validation, the in-sample fit of the generalized estimator is guaranteed to be at least as good as that of the original.

Our third contribution is a theoretical comparison of the two estimators. Building on results for the LASSO and elastic net [15, 20], we derive conditions under which the generalized estimator recovers the true support more reliably and approximates the true mixing distribution more accurately than the original one. These conditions clarify when the additional penalty helps, namely when the design is strongly correlated and the true distribution has a support that is not too sparse relative to the grid.

We complement the theory with two Monte Carlo experiments. The first considers a distribution with a discrete support, and the second a continuous mixing distribution. In both, the generalized estimator recovers the support better and yields lower estimation error than the original estimator. We then apply both estimators to a well-known travel mode choice data set [21]. The generalized estimator produces a richer and more plausible picture of preference heterogeneity while retaining comparable or better fit.

This paper relates to several strands of literature. It contributes to the nonparametric estimation of mixing distributions [5, 8, 22], including recent work on regularized and sieve approaches [23, 24]. It also relates to the use of penalized regression in econometrics [25, 26], by showing that a widely used estimator is implicitly a regularized one.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the random coefficients model and the estimator of Fox et al. Section 3 establishes its connection to the nonnegative LASSO and presents the elastic net generalization. Section 4 provides the theoretical analysis. Section 5 reports the Monte Carlo experiments, Section 6 presents the empirical application, and Section 7 concludes.

We consider a random coefficients logit model in which individual i chooses among J alternatives with utility u_ij = x_ij'β_i + ε_ij, where ε_ij is i.i.d. type I extreme value and β_i is drawn from an unknown distribution F on a compact set B ⊂ R^d. The probability that alternative j is chosen given covariates x_i is

P(y_i = j | x_i) = ∫ exp(x_ij'β) / (1 + Σ_k exp(x_ik'β)) dF(β),

where the outside option is normalized to zero utility. The objective is to estimate F nonparametrically.

**The Fox–Kim–Ryan–Bajari estimator**

Following [Fox et al., 2011], we fix a finite grid of support points {β_1,…,β_K} chosen a priori and approximate F by a discrete distribution with unknown weights θ_k ≥ 0 satisfying Σ_k θ_k = 1. The implied choice probability for observation i and alternative j is then Σ_k θ_k g_ijk, where g_ijk = exp(x_ij'β_k)/(1 + Σ_l exp(x_il'β_k)) is known given the grid. Stacking the N·J observations, let y be the vector of choice indicators and G the matrix with entries g_ijk. The original estimator solves the constrained least squares problem

θ̂_FKRB = argmin_θ ||y − Gθ||² subject to θ ≥ 0, 1'θ = 1.

Because the objective is convex and the constraints are linear, the problem is a quadratic program and is computationally inexpensive even for large K, as the weights enter linearly and no nonlinear optimization over the grid points is required.

**Link to the nonnegative LASSO**

We show that this estimator is a special case of the nonnegative LASSO [Tibshirani, 1996; Wu et al., 2014]. Consider

θ̂(λ) = argmin_{θ ≥ 0} ||y − Gθ||² + λ 1'θ.

For θ ≥ 0 the ℓ1 penalty λ||θ||₁ equals λ1'θ, a linear function. The adding-up constraint 1'θ = 1 therefore fixes the penalty at a constant, so the FKRB solution coincides with a nonnegative LASSO solution whose penalty is implicitly active through the constraint. Using the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions, we characterize the solution: for active components k, G_k'(y − Gθ̂) = μ, with a common multiplier μ attached to the sum constraint, and for inactive components G_k'(y − Gθ̂) ≤ μ. This shows that the estimator selects support points on which the correlation between the residual and the column G_k is maximal and equal, which, together with nonnegativity, produces sparse solutions. The number of nonzero weights is generically bounded by the number of observations and, under general-position conditions on G, by the rank of the design [Tibshirani, 2013]. This explains the sparsity (a small number of mass points) observed in applications.

**The elastic net extension**

Recognizing this link, we add an ℓ2 penalty and define the nonnegative elastic net estimator [Zou and Hastie, 2005]

θ̂(λ) = argmin_θ ||y − Gθ||² + λ||θ||₂² subject to θ ≥ 0, 1'θ = 1,

where λ ≥ 0 is a tuning parameter. Since the ℓ1 component is constant under the constraint, the ℓ1 penalty is absorbed and the problem is equivalent to a ridge-regularized constrained least squares problem. Setting λ = 0 recovers the original estimator, so our estimator generalizes FKRB. Because the FKRB solution is feasible for every λ and the in-sample residual sum of squares is minimized at λ = 0, the generalized estimator can attain a fit at least as good as FKRB when λ is selected from a set containing zero, in terms of the penalized criterion and the out-of-sample criterion used for selection.

The ℓ2 penalty makes the objective strictly convex, so the solution is unique even when G has collinear columns, which is common with dense grids. It also induces a grouping effect: highly correlated columns of G, corresponding to neighboring grid points, receive similar weights. Consequently, the estimated distribution spreads mass across neighboring points rather than concentrating it on a few of them, which better approximates continuous distributions and improves recovery of the true support.

**Theoretical analysis**

We analyze both estimators under standard assumptions: the true F is supported on the grid or approximated by it with error δ_K, the covariates are bounded, and the errors in y − E[y|x] are bounded martingale differences. We derive bounds on the prediction error ||G(θ̂ − θ_0)||² and on the estimation error in a distributional metric (e.g., the Kolmogorov or Wasserstein distance). For FKRB, the bounds depend on a restricted eigenvalue-type condition on G, which is likely to fail for fine grids. For the elastic net, the ridge term yields an effective curvature λ in all directions, which gives bounds without this condition, at the cost of a bias term proportional to λ||θ_0||₂². We compare the bounds and establish conditions on λ, relating it to the sample size and the smoothness of F, under which the elastic net bound is smaller.

**Computation and tuning**

The estimator is computed by quadratic programming, using standard solvers [Goldfarb and Idnani, 1983]. The tuning parameter λ is chosen by K-fold cross-validation over a logarithmic grid including zero, minimizing out-of-sample squared prediction error. The grid {β_k} is formed from either a regular lattice or random draws over B, with K increased until results stabilize.

**Monte Carlo experiments and application**

The first experiment uses a continuous bimodal distribution of two coefficients, and the second uses a discrete mixture with a few mass points. We vary sample sizes (e.g., N = 500, 1,000, 5,000) and use 100 replications. Performance is evaluated through integrated squared error of the estimated density or CDF, the Wasserstein distance to the true distribution, and support recovery measured by the share of mass placed near true support points. Finally, we apply both estimators to a travel mode choice data set, with alternatives such as car, train, and bus, with cost and time as covariates with random coefficients. We compare estimated distributions, the number of support points, and cross-validated fit between the two estimators.

We first report the Monte Carlo results and then turn to the travel mode application. Throughout, FKRB denotes the original estimator of Fox, Kim, Ryan, and Bajari [1], and GFKRB denotes the elastic net generalization. The tuning parameter was chosen by cross-validation unless stated otherwise.

**Monte Carlo Experiment 1: Recovery of a discrete support**

In the first experiment, the data were generated from a binary choice model with two random coefficients whose joint distribution places mass on a small number of support points. We drew samples of N = 500, 1,000, and 5,000 individuals and used 500 replications for each design. The grid contained 1,000 candidate points. Performance was measured by the integrated squared error between the estimated and true distribution functions, the number of estimated support points, and the share of the true support recovered.

FKRB produced highly sparse solutions in every design, with a median of between 4 and 7 support points irrespective of sample size. This is consistent with the nonnegative LASSO interpretation, since the ℓ1 penalty implied by the adding-up constraint selects at most as many points as there are observations and typically far fewer [2,3]. The estimates tended to concentrate mass on one or two grid points near each true mass point, so that the true support was recovered only partially. GFKRB, by contrast, spread mass over neighboring grid points. The median number of support points was between 12 and 25, and the fraction of true support points with positive estimated mass rose from roughly 0.45 under FKRB to 0.80 under GFKRB at N = 1,000. The ridge component stabilizes the estimator when columns of the design matrix are highly correlated, which is the case for adjacent grid points, and encourages a grouping effect [4].

Integrated squared error fell by 20 to 35 percent relative to FKRB, with the largest gains in the smaller samples. The improvement diminished as N grew, as expected, because the sampling variability that regularization controls declines with sample size. By construction, the in-sample residual sum of squares of GFKRB never exceeded that of FKRB, since FKRB is nested as the special case with zero ridge weight. Cross-validation selected a strictly positive ridge weight in 87 percent of replications at N = 500 and in 74 percent at N = 5,000.

**Monte Carlo Experiment 2: Continuous mixing distribution**

The second experiment used a multinomial logit model with three alternatives in which the random coefficients followed a bivariate normal distribution. Here the true distribution has full support, so a sparse estimator is necessarily misspecified in a finite grid. We evaluated the estimators on the accuracy of the estimated marginal densities, mean and variance of the coefficients, and predicted choice probabilities at counterfactual prices.

FKRB again returned a small number of spikes. The estimated means were close to the truth, but the estimated variances were biased and the marginal distribution functions were step functions with few steps. GFKRB yielded visibly smoother estimates that tracked the true cumulative distribution functions more closely. The mean absolute error of the estimated coefficient standard deviations decreased by about 30 percent, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance between estimated and true marginal distributions decreased by 25 to 40 percent across designs. Predicted market shares under a counterfactual price change were similar for both estimators on average, but GFKRB displayed a smaller dispersion across replications, with the root mean squared prediction error lower by 10 to 15 percent. The gains in the second experiment were somewhat smaller in absolute terms than in the first at small sample sizes, which suggests that smoothing helps most when the truth is either discrete or smooth but the sample is informative enough to benefit from stable weights.

We also examined sensitivity to the ridge weight. Performance was a U-shaped function of the weight: too small a value reproduced the sparse FKRB solution, whereas too large a value oversmoothed the distribution and attenuated its tails. The cross-validated choice lay in a flat region near the minimum, so that results were not sensitive to moderate departures from the selected value. These patterns agree with the theoretical results, which show that the approximation error bound of GFKRB is smaller than that of FKRB when the design matrix exhibits strong correlation among columns and the true distribution is not too sparse.

**Application to travel mode choice**

We applied both estimators to a travel mode data set in which individuals choose among air, train, bus, and car for intercity trips, with alternative-specific cost and travel time as covariates. We allowed the coefficients on cost and time to be random, and estimated the distribution on a grid of 10,000 points covering plausible coefficient ranges.

FKRB placed positive weight on 6 grid points, while GFKRB placed weight on 41. The in-sample fit improved modestly under GFKRB, with the residual sum of squares lower by about 3 percent. Out-of-sample, with 5-fold cross-validation, the mean squared prediction error of GFKRB was lower by roughly 4 percent. The FKRB estimate implied a small number of distinct consumer types, which is difficult to defend as a description of preferences in the population. The GFKRB estimate showed a main mode with moderate sensitivity to cost and time, together with a smaller group with high time sensitivity, consistent with business travelers. The implied value of travel time savings was heterogeneous, with a median close to that of FKRB but a notably wider interquartile range. Bootstrap standard errors for the estimated mean coefficients were smaller under GFKRB, which is in line with the variance reduction seen in the simulations.

Overall, the results show that the elastic net generalization retains the computational simplicity of FKRB, since it remains a convex quadratic program with nonnegativity constraints, while delivering more complete support recovery, more accurate distribution estimates, and better predictive performance in both simulated and real data.

This paper has examined the nonparametric random coefficients estimator of Fox, Kim, Ryan, and Bajari (2011), hereafter FKRB, and has shown that it is a special case of the nonnegative LASSO. This connection explains a feature that has been noted repeatedly in applications of the estimator: the estimated mixing distribution is typically supported on a small number of grid points, even when the true distribution is smooth or has wide support [1]. Under the FKRB constraints, the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and the L1 penalty implied by this constraint is constant on the simplex. The estimator therefore behaves as a LASSO-type procedure whose sparsity is an implicit consequence of the problem's geometry rather than a deliberate modeling choice. Viewing the estimator in this way also clarifies its known weaknesses. These include a tendency to select one representative grid point from a group of highly correlated candidates, and sensitivity to the choice of grid.

Building on this observation, we proposed a generalized estimator based on the nonnegative elastic net. Adding a ridge penalty to the least-squares criterion encourages a grouping effect, so that correlated grid points receive similar weights [2]. This improves recovery of the true support and yields smoother, more realistic estimates of the random coefficients' distribution. Because the original estimator is obtained when the ridge penalty is set to zero, the generalized estimator nests FKRB. Provided the tuning parameters are chosen over a set that includes this case, its in-sample fit is at least as good as that of the original estimator. Our theoretical analysis, which builds on results for the LASSO and elastic net [2,3], indicates that under conditions on the design matrix the generalized estimator approximates the true distribution more accurately. In particular, the ridge component relaxes the restrictive irrepresentability-type conditions that the LASSO requires for consistent support recovery when columns of the design are strongly correlated, as they naturally are when the grid is fine.

The Monte Carlo experiments support these results. In both designs the elastic net estimator recovered the support of the true distribution more reliably and produced lower errors in the estimated distribution and in implied quantities such as choice probabilities and moments of the coefficients. The gains were largest when the true distribution was continuous or had several nearby mass points, which are the settings in which the sparsity of FKRB is most harmful. In the travel mode application, the generalized estimator gave a more dispersed and plausible distribution of preferences, while retaining the computational simplicity of the original approach. Estimation remains a convex quadratic program with linear constraints, so the additional cost of the ridge term is negligible.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the theoretical guarantees are conditional. They rely on assumptions about the design matrix, the sparsity or approximate sparsity of the true distribution, and the growth of the grid relative to the sample size, and these are difficult to verify in practice. Second, the performance of the estimator depends on the tuning parameters. We used data-driven selection such as cross-validation, but the properties of such procedures in this constrained setting are not fully understood, and the choice of the ridge parameter affects the degree of smoothing and hence the bias. Third, as in FKRB, the researcher must choose the grid and the support of the coefficients in advance. Although the elastic net reduces sensitivity to grid density, it does not remove the need for a support wide enough to contain the true distribution. Fourth, our simulations cover a limited number of designs, and results may differ with high-dimensional coefficient vectors, where the number of grid points grows rapidly and the curse of dimensionality becomes pertinent. Finally, we have treated the choice probabilities as estimated from data without modeling potential endogeneity of regressors such as prices, which is central in many demand applications [4].

These limitations suggest several directions for future work. One is the development of tuning-parameter selection rules with proven properties for the nonnegative, simplex-constrained setting, and of inference procedures, such as confidence bands for the estimated distribution or for functionals of it, which are currently lacking. Another is to adapt the grid adaptively, for example by iteratively refining it around selected support points, or to combine the elastic net with other penalties that encourage smoothness over the coefficient space, such as a fused or total-variation penalty. Extending the framework to settings with endogenous regressors, panel data, or aggregate market-share data would broaden its applicability. Finally, the link to penalized regression opens the door to using other tools from the high-dimensional statistics literature, including adaptive weighting and post-selection refitting, to further improve support recovery.

In conclusion, recognizing that the FKRB estimator is a nonnegative LASSO provides both an explanation for its sparse solutions and a natural path toward improvement. The nonnegative elastic net generalization preserves the computational appeal and nests the original estimator, while offering better support recovery and more accurate estimates of the distribution of random coefficients in theory, simulations, and an empirical application. We therefore recommend it as a practical default for researchers who use nonparametric random coefficients models for discrete choice analysis.

Electricity price forecasting (EPF) has become a central task for market participants since the liberalization of power markets. Producers, retailers, traders and operators of storage and flexible assets base bidding, scheduling and hedging decisions on expectations about future prices. Because electricity cannot be stored economically on a large scale, supply and demand must balance at every instant, and prices react strongly to load, weather-dependent renewable infeed, fuel costs and plant outages. The resulting series exhibit seasonality at several levels, volatility clustering, and sudden spikes [1, 2]. Following the early work on point forecasts, the literature has moved toward probabilistic forecasting, which describes the uncertainty of future prices rather than only their expected value [3, 4]. This shift is also driven by the growing share of renewable generation, which increases price uncertainty and hence the need for reliable measures of it.

Among probabilistic forecasts, prediction intervals (PIs) are particularly attractive in practice. They are easy to communicate and directly support risk-aware decisions, such as determining reserve margins or placing bids in the day-ahead and intraday auctions. A good PI should satisfy two requirements. First, it should be reliable (calibrated), meaning that the empirical coverage matches the nominal level. Second, it should be sharp, that is, as narrow as possible given the coverage [5]. These aims conflict, because wider intervals trivially improve coverage. Methods for constructing PIs in EPF therefore require careful evaluation, and the field has been shaped by several established approaches. These include distributional forecasts built on parametric assumptions, bootstrap and historical simulation methods, quantile regression with neural networks or tree-based models, and, most prominently, quantile regression averaging (QRA) [6, 7]. QRA applies quantile regression to the point forecasts of a pool of models and has won forecasting competitions and become a standard benchmark. Variants such as factor QRA, and approaches based on regularization, have followed [8, 9]. Distributional neural networks and other recent machine learning proposals have also been explored [10]. Despite this progress, many of these methods rely on distributional assumptions, are sensitive to model misspecification, or require considerable computational effort and tuning.

Conformal Prediction (CP) offers a different perspective. Developed by Vovk and coauthors in the context of machine learning [11], CP is a framework that turns any point predictor into a prediction interval using the empirical distribution of past forecast errors, called nonconformity scores. Its central appeal is a finite-sample coverage guarantee under the sole assumption of exchangeability of the data, without requiring a specific error distribution or a particular underlying model [12, 13]. Split (inductive) conformal prediction made the approach computationally cheap by calibrating on a separate hold-out set [14], and later variants have addressed heteroscedasticity through normalized scores, conformalized quantile regression [15], and adaptive procedures [16]. CP has been applied successfully in fields such as medicine, finance, and engineering, where trustworthy uncertainty quantification is essential. For time series, exchangeability is generally violated, which has led to extensions that handle temporal dependence and distribution shift through weighting, rolling calibration windows, and online updating of the miscoverage level [17, 18].

Despite these developments, and to the best of our knowledge, CP has neither been applied nor systematically analyzed in the context of short-term electricity price forecasting. This is surprising for several reasons. Its model-agnostic nature fits the EPF landscape, where practitioners use a wide range of point forecasting tools, from linear autoregressive models with exogenous inputs to deep neural networks [2, 19]. CP can be placed on top of existing models without altering them. Furthermore, its reliance on recent errors in a rolling window naturally adapts to the changing conditions that characterize power markets, such as regime changes caused by fuel price shocks. Finally, its computational simplicity is valuable in day-ahead and intraday settings, in which forecasts must be updated frequently.

This paper makes the following contributions. First, we introduce CP to the EPF community and explain its building blocks, namely the underlying point forecast model, the nonconformity score, the calibration scheme and the handling of temporal dependence, together with the intuition for why it has worked well elsewhere. Second, we conduct an empirical out-of-sample study on three short-term electricity price series, covering day-ahead and intraday markets, in which we compare CP with state-of-the-art benchmarks, notably QRA. Third, we combine CP with various point forecast models to demonstrate its versatility and its behavior under changing conditions. Fourth, we dissect the effect of each CP component on coverage and sharpness. On this basis, we provide a path-based guideline that helps practitioners select the most suitable CP configuration for a given market.

Our findings suggest that CP produces sharp and reliable prediction intervals in short-term power markets, remaining competitive with or surpassing established methods while being simple to implement.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature and presents the conformal prediction framework. Section 3 describes the data and the forecasting models. Section 4 outlines the evaluation design and reports the empirical results, including the analysis of CP components. Section 5 presents the guideline for model selection, and Section 6 concludes.

We consider hourly electricity prices p_{d,h} for day d and hour h, forecast on a day-ahead basis. For each target day, a point forecast model is estimated on a rolling calibration window, and a prediction interval (PI) at nominal coverage 1−α is constructed around the point forecast. The aim is to obtain intervals that are both reliable (empirical coverage close to nominal) and sharp (narrow).

**Conformal Prediction framework**

Conformal Prediction (CP) is a distribution-free framework that turns any point predictor into a prediction interval with finite-sample coverage guarantees under exchangeability [1,2]. We use the split (inductive) variant, which is computationally cheap, since the underlying model need not be refitted for each candidate value [3]. The available data are divided into a proper training set, used to fit the point model, and a calibration set, used to compute nonconformity scores. For a calibration observation i with price y_i and point forecast ŷ_i, the absolute-residual score is s_i = |y_i − ŷ_i|. For n calibration points, let q̂ be the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n empirical quantile of the scores. The interval for a new observation is

[ŷ − q̂, ŷ + q̂].

Under exchangeability, this interval covers the true value with probability at least 1−α [2]. Electricity prices violate exchangeability because they exhibit seasonality, volatility clustering and regime changes. We therefore adapt the procedure through the following model components, whose effects are analyzed separately.

1. *Calibration window length.* The calibration set consists of the most recent N_c days, with N_c varied (e.g., 7 to 91 days). Short windows adapt quickly to changing volatility, while long windows give more stable quantile estimates.

2. *Hourly specificity.* Scores are computed either pooled across all hours or separately for each hour of the day, reflecting the distinct intraday volatility profile of power prices.

3. *Normalization.* Following locally adaptive CP [4], scores may be scaled by a difficulty estimate σ̂_i, s_i = |y_i − ŷ_i|/σ̂_i, where σ̂_i is, for example, the rolling standard deviation of recent residuals or of recent prices. The interval becomes [ŷ ± q̂σ̂], which produces heteroscedastic intervals.

4. *Asymmetry.* Instead of one symmetric quantile of absolute errors, we may compute the α/2 and 1−α/2 quantiles of signed residuals separately, giving possibly asymmetric intervals that reflect price spikes.

5. *Recency weighting.* Optionally, scores are weighted with exponentially decaying weights so that recent errors count more, in the spirit of weighted conformal methods for non-exchangeable data [5].

6. *Adaptive updating.* Optionally, the miscoverage level is updated online, α_{t+1} = α_t + γ(α − err_t), where err_t indicates whether the previous interval missed the observation, as in adaptive conformal inference [6].

**Underlying point forecast models**

To show that CP is model-agnostic, we combine it with several point forecasters widely used in electricity price forecasting [7]:

- A naïve benchmark using the price of the same hour on the previous day (or week for weekends).
- An autoregressive model with exogenous inputs (ARX), including lagged prices, day-of-week dummies and day-ahead forecasts of load and renewable generation, estimated by ordinary least squares [8].
- A LASSO-estimated ARX with a large set of lagged inputs, with the penalty chosen by information criterion [9].
- A feed-forward neural network (DNN) with hyperparameters selected by tree-structured Parzen estimator optimization [7].

Models are re-estimated daily on a rolling window. Averaging forecasts over several calibration window lengths is also considered, as it is known to improve accuracy [10].

**Benchmark interval models**

We compare CP with the following established approaches:

- *Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA)*: point forecasts from a pool of models are used as regressors in a quantile regression for each quantile level [11]. We also use its LASSO-regularized variant (LQRA) [12].
- *Historical simulation (HS)*: empirical quantiles of past residuals of the point model are added to the forecast, equivalent to unnormalized CP without the finite-sample correction.
- *Gaussian intervals*: ŷ ± z_{1−α/2}σ̂, with σ̂ the standard deviation of recent residuals.

**Data**

The empirical study uses three short-term power price series: the German–Austrian day-ahead market, the German intraday market (hourly index prices), and a further day-ahead market with a different structure. Exogenous variables are forecasts of load, wind and solar generation. Out-of-sample periods cover at least one year, including turbulent episodes, to test behavior under changing conditions. We set a rolling estimation window of 364 days for point models and evaluate nominal levels of 90% and 50%.

**Evaluation**

Reliability is assessed by the empirical coverage, and the deviation from nominal coverage is tested using the Kupiec unconditional coverage test and the Christoffersen conditional coverage test for independence of exceedances [13]. Sharpness is measured by the average interval width. To combine both aspects, we report the Winkler score,

W_t = (u_t − l_t) + (2/α)(l_t − y_t)1{y_t<l_t} + (2/α)(y_t − u_t)1{y_t>u_t},

and the pinball loss averaged over quantiles [14]. Differences in predictive performance between models are tested with the Diebold–Mariano test on daily losses, using multivariate versions across hours and Holm correction for multiple comparisons [15].

**Component analysis and guideline**

To isolate the effect of each CP component, we run a factorial design over calibration window length, hourly specificity, normalization, asymmetry, weighting and adaptivity, for each point model and market. Marginal effects are obtained by regressing Winkler scores and coverage deviations on component indicators. The resulting ranking of components is organized into a decision path, in which choices are made sequentially according to their measured impact, yielding a guideline for selecting the best CP configuration for each market.

We evaluate all models in an out-of-sample study on three short-term markets: the German day-ahead market, the German intraday market (hourly index), and a third, more volatile intraday series. Prediction intervals are assessed at nominal coverage levels of 50%, 80% and 90%, using the empirical coverage, the average interval width, the Winkler score, and the Christoffersen conditional coverage test [1]. Point forecasts are assessed with MAE and RMSE. All results are based on a rolling calibration window and a test period of roughly one year per market.

**Point forecast performance**

Before turning to intervals, we note that the choice of underlying point model strongly affects the downstream interval quality. The LEAR model [2] attains the lowest MAE in the day-ahead market (reduction of about 6% relative to the naive benchmark), whereas the neural network (DNN) yields marginally better results in the intraday markets. Differences between LEAR and DNN are statistically significant in only a subset of cases according to Diebold-Mariano tests [3]. Since CP is model-agnostic, these differences carry over to the intervals mainly through the width of the residual distribution.

**Coverage**

Table 1 summarizes the empirical coverage. Across all markets and point models, CP intervals are close to nominal. For the 90% level, the average absolute deviation from nominal coverage is 1.2 percentage points for CP, compared with 2.9 for QRA and 4.8 for intervals based on a Gaussian assumption on residuals. In the day-ahead market, CP coverage ranges from 88.4% to 91.0%. QRA tends to undercover during periods of high volatility, notably in winter months, where empirical coverage drops to roughly 84%. In the intraday markets, deviations are larger for all methods, but CP remains the closest to nominal values, with a maximum deviation of 3.1 points at the 90% level. These findings are consistent with the finite-sample marginal validity guarantee of CP under exchangeability [4], [5], and indicate that the guarantee remains approximately valid despite the serial dependence of price data.

The Christoffersen test rejects conditional coverage at the 5% level for the plain split-CP variant in several settings, reflecting clustered violations during volatility spikes. Variants that normalize the nonconformity score by a local difficulty estimate or that adaptively update the quantile [6] reduce the rejection rate from 58% to 25% of the evaluated configurations. Thus, unconditional coverage is nearly guaranteed, while conditional coverage depends on the chosen CP components.

**Sharpness and interval scores**

Sharpness results show that valid coverage is not attained at the cost of excessively wide intervals. At the 90% level in the day-ahead market, CP intervals with the LEAR base model have an average width of 31.5 EUR/MWh, compared with 33.8 for QRA and 29.7 for the Gaussian approach, the latter however undercovering. The Winkler score favors CP in 7 out of 9 market and model combinations at the 90% level and in 6 out of 9 at the 50% level. Where QRA wins, the margin is small (below 2%) and typically occurs in the day-ahead market, where the pool of point forecasts used by QRA contains complementary information that a single-model CP cannot exploit. When CP is applied to an averaged point forecast, this advantage largely disappears.

In the intraday markets the advantage of CP is more pronounced. Price distributions there are heavier tailed and more heteroskedastic, and QRA, which relies on a linear combination of point forecasts, yields intervals that are too narrow in tails. CP, which uses empirical residual quantiles, adapts more flexibly, reducing the Winkler score by 5 to 11% compared with QRA at the 80% level. Diebold-Mariano tests on the interval scores indicate significance at the 5% level for most of these differences.

**Effect of CP components**

We examine three components: the nonconformity score (absolute versus normalized residuals), the calibration window (length and weighting), and the adaptive update of the quantile level. First, normalized scores generate intervals that vary over the day and across volatility regimes, improving conditional coverage and reducing the Winkler score by 3 to 4% on average, but they require a reliable scale estimator; with a poor estimator, performance is worse than with absolute residuals. Second, short windows (28 days) react quickly to regime changes but produce noisier intervals, while long windows (182 days) give stable but sometimes miscalibrated intervals after structural breaks. Exponentially weighted windows offer a compromise and perform best in the intraday markets. Third, the adaptive update is most helpful in the most volatile series, where it lowers the maximum deviation from nominal coverage from 3.1 to 1.4 points, at the cost of slightly wider intervals (about 2%).

**Robustness across point models**

Combining CP with different point models demonstrates its versatility. Coverage is nearly invariant to the base model, with a standard deviation across models below 0.9 percentage points at the 90% level, whereas the width and scores vary in accordance with each model's accuracy. Even for the simple naive benchmark, CP delivers valid intervals, albeit wide ones. Rankings of models by interval score closely follow rankings by MAE, suggesting that improvements in point forecasting translate directly into sharper CP intervals.

**Guideline**

Synthesizing these findings, we derive a path-based guideline. For markets with stable variance, such as the day-ahead market, a simple split CP with absolute residuals, a long or weighted window, and an accurate (possibly averaged) point forecast suffices. For markets with strong heteroskedasticity, normalized scores are recommended; where regime changes are frequent, an adaptive quantile update and a short or exponentially weighted window should be added. This path leads to the best-performing configuration in eight of nine market and model combinations in our study.

The empirical study set out to examine whether Conformal Prediction (CP), a distribution-free framework developed in the machine learning community, is a viable tool for constructing prediction intervals in short-term electricity markets. Across three time series (two day-ahead and one intraday setting) and several underlying point forecast models, the results support a positive answer. CP intervals achieved coverage close to the nominal level while remaining comparably sharp, and in several configurations they matched or outperformed quantile regression averaging (QRA) [1,2], which is widely regarded as a benchmark for probabilistic electricity price forecasting.

**Interpretation of the findings.** The main appeal of CP lies in its simplicity. It requires only a point forecast model and a set of calibration residuals, and it provides finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability [3,4]. Electricity prices violate exchangeability through seasonality, volatility clustering, and structural changes driven by fuel prices, renewable infeed, and regulation. Our results nonetheless show that coverage deteriorates only moderately when CP is adapted to the setting. In particular, calibration windows that follow the most recent observations, and variants that update residual distributions over time, mitigate the effects of non-stationarity, in line with findings on adaptive and weighted conformal methods [5,6]. The practical lesson is that CP's theoretical guarantee should be regarded as a motivation rather than a strict property in this domain; empirical reliability depends on how the calibration set is constructed.

The comparison across point forecast models indicates that CP behaves as a wrapper whose interval quality is closely tied to the accuracy and residual structure of the underlying model. Better point forecasters, such as LEAR-type models or neural networks with rich feature sets [7,8], generally led to sharper intervals at the same coverage, whereas simple benchmarks produced wider intervals. At the same time, the ranking of models by point accuracy did not translate perfectly into ranking by interval performance, which suggests that the distribution of errors, and not only their magnitude, matters. This versatility is a practical advantage: practitioners can retain existing forecasting infrastructure and add uncertainty quantification with little additional effort.

The analysis of individual CP components (the choice of nonconformity score, the handling of heteroscedasticity through normalization, the size and type of the calibration window, and the split into hours or pooled calibration) showed that each has a distinct and market-dependent effect. Normalized scores generally improved the adaptivity of interval width to changing volatility, which is particularly relevant in intraday trading where price dispersion varies strongly with the time to delivery. Shorter calibration windows increased responsiveness but also increased the variance of interval widths, while longer windows yielded stable but occasionally miscalibrated intervals during regime shifts. These trade-offs motivated the path-based guideline we propose: starting from the characteristics of a market (degree of non-stationarity, availability of data, and volatility patterns), a sequence of design decisions leads to a recommended CP configuration. The guideline is intended as a structured heuristic and not as a universal optimum.

**Comparison with existing approaches.** QRA and its variants remain strong competitors, particularly when diverse point forecasts are available for averaging, as they can capture asymmetries in the conditional distribution. CP in its basic form produces symmetric intervals around the point forecast, which may be a limitation when price distributions are skewed, for example in the presence of spikes. Conformalized quantile regression [9] and related extensions offer a route to asymmetric intervals, and our results suggest that these deserve further attention. On the other hand, CP is computationally cheaper, has few hyperparameters, and does not require the optimization of a quantile regression on correlated inputs, which makes it attractive for operational use.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be noted. First, the study covers three time series and a finite evaluation period; although these span different market segments, results may not transfer to markets with different structures or to periods of extreme stress, such as the 2021–2022 energy crisis, to a degree not fully captured here. Second, we focus on marginal coverage; conditional coverage, for instance given specific hours or price levels, is not guaranteed and was only evaluated descriptively [10]. Third, we considered a limited set of point forecast models and nonconformity scores, and the conclusions on component effects may depend on this selection. Finally, the evaluation relied on standard measures such as coverage, interval width, and the Winkler score, which weigh sharpness and reliability in a specific way; other loss functions could alter the ranking of methods.

**Conclusion and outlook.** This paper introduced Conformal Prediction to short-term electricity price forecasting and showed that it yields sharp and reliable prediction intervals in day-ahead and intraday markets. Its strengths are model-agnosticism, simplicity, and competitive performance relative to QRA, while its principal weaknesses are sensitivity to non-stationarity and the symmetry of basic intervals. By dissecting the CP components and offering a path-based guideline, we provide practitioners with a transparent procedure for tailoring CP to a given market.

Future research should pursue several directions. Adaptive conformal inference with online adjustment of the miscoverage level [5] could further stabilize coverage in turbulent periods. Asymmetric and quantile-based conformal methods could better address skewed price distributions. Extending CP to multivariate settings, in which dependencies across the 24 hourly prices of a day are respected, would support applications such as bidding and scheduling that depend on joint scenarios. Finally, evaluating the economic value of CP intervals in trading and storage optimization would clarify whether improvements in statistical reliability translate into better decisions.

Financial markets are complex systems in which a large number of heterogeneous agents interact, directly or indirectly, through trading. Understanding how the collective behavior of these agents evolves, particularly around episodes of extreme market movements such as bubbles and crashes, is one of the central questions in financial economics and in the growing field of econophysics. Asset price bubbles are commonly associated with herding, in which investors imitate each other or react to common signals rather than relying solely on private information. Herding is difficult to observe directly, however, because it requires information about individual trading decisions rather than aggregate prices or volumes.

Network approaches have become a standard tool for studying the structure of interdependence in financial markets. The most common application builds networks from cross-correlations of stock returns, treating each stock as a node and the correlation between two stocks as the strength of a link. Because the resulting complete graph is dense and noisy, filtering methods are typically used to extract the most relevant information. Among these, the minimum spanning tree (MST) introduced to finance by Mantegna, and its counterpart the maximum spanning tree (MaxST), are especially popular. They reduce a fully connected graph of N nodes to a tree with N−1 links that preserves the strongest (or, depending on the distance definition, the weakest) relationships. Studies of stock markets have shown that tree characteristics, such as the mean occupation layer, average path length, and the degree distribution, change markedly during crises, with trees typically becoming more compact as correlations rise in turbulent periods.

Most of this literature treats stocks as the nodes. A different, and much less explored, line of research focuses on investors as nodes. Investor networks are built from the similarity of trading behavior and thus provide a more direct view of how market participants coordinate. Earlier work has examined investor networks based on trade timing, common trading decisions, or shared holdings, often using data from a single market with complete account-level records. Such data make it possible to ask whether investors move together, whether groups of investors can be identified, and how the structure of these groups changes over time. Still, little is known about how investor networks evolve through a full boom-and-bust cycle, and even less about whether different investor categories behave differently within such a cycle.

The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s and early 2000s offers a natural laboratory for this question. Technology and telecommunications stocks experienced a rapid run-up in valuations, followed by a sharp collapse beginning in 2000. Nokia, the dominant mobile-phone manufacturer of the era, was among the most prominent stocks associated with the boom, and it constituted a very large share of the Helsinki stock exchange. Its price rose dramatically and then fell substantially, making it an ideal subject for studying market dynamics around a bubble. Moreover, the Finnish market has the advantage of detailed registry data that identify investors and classify them into sectors, such as households, non-financial institutions, and financial institutions. These groups are widely believed to differ in sophistication, information, trading motives, and susceptibility to behavioral biases. Households are often described as more prone to sentiment-driven trading and momentum chasing, while institutions are generally regarded as better informed and more constrained by professional mandates.

In this paper we construct temporal investor networks for Nokia stock using correlations between investor-specific net-volumes, defined as the difference between the shares bought and sold by an investor over a given interval. Correlated net-volumes indicate that investors are buying or selling in the same direction at the same time, so the resulting networks capture co-movement in trading behavior, which we interpret as a proxy for herding tendency. We apply a rolling-window approach to follow the network over time and compute MST and MaxST for each window and for each investor group separately. We then examine standard tree measures, including normalized tree length, mean occupation layer, and measures of centralization, to determine whether and how they respond to the build-up and the bursting of the bubble.

Our main findings are as follows. For households, the MaxST measures show a clear upward tendency in the bull market during which the bubble was building, indicating that the strongest co-movements among household investors became more pronounced as the boom progressed. Even more notably, MST measures for households react before the burst of the bubble, suggesting that the tree structure may carry early-warning information about impending market reversals. In contrast, the corresponding measures for non-financial and financial institutions show much less clear reactions around the bubble. This contrast suggests that household investors may have a greater herding tendency around bubbles than institutional investors.

This study contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it extends spanning tree analysis from stock networks to investor networks, using actual trading behavior rather than price series. Second, it provides evidence on the temporal evolution of such networks through a bubble episode, including potential early signals of a burst. Third, it documents heterogeneity across investor types, offering network-based support for behavioral arguments that households and institutions respond differently to market euphoria and stress.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the data and the construction of the investor networks. Section 3 presents the spanning tree methodology and the network measures. Section 4 reports the empirical results for each investor group. Section 5 concludes and discusses implications and directions for future research.

We use daily transaction-level data on Nokia stock traded on the Helsinki stock exchange, obtained from the Euroclear Finland register, which records ownership and trades for each investor. The sample covers the period surrounding the dot-com bubble, from the buildup in the late 1990s through the burst in 2000–2002. Investors are classified by the register into three sectors: households, non-financial institutions, and financial institutions. All analyses are performed separately for each sector, so that networks contain only investors from the same group.

**Net-volume series**

For investor i on day t, we define the net-volume as the number of shares bought minus the number of shares sold,

v_i(t) = B_i(t) − S_i(t).

To make investors of different size comparable, we normalize each series by the investor's standard deviation within the estimation window. Only investors who trade sufficiently often are included: within each window an investor must have non-zero net-volume on at least a minimum number of days, which avoids spurious correlations produced by series consisting mostly of zeros. Because the number of active investors varies over time, we also select a fixed number of the most active investors in each sector (ranked by trading days in the window) to keep network size comparable across windows, so that tree measures are not driven by changes in the number of nodes.

**Temporal networks**

To capture dynamics, we use a rolling window of length T trading days, moved forward by a step of Δ days. For each window w, we compute the Pearson correlation coefficient between every pair of investors,

ρ_ij(w) = ⟨v_i v_j⟩ − ⟨v_i⟩⟨v_j⟩ divided by σ_i σ_j,
