The central result in this literature is that, with exogenously fixed prices, information aggregates asymptotically if and only if private signals are unbounded, meaning that arbitrarily strong signals occur with positive probability. With bounded signals, herds form and learning is incomplete.

That benchmark abstracts from a feature of nearly every real market: prices are set by firms that understand how consumers learn. A seller facing a sequence of consumers who infer quality from past purchases has strong incentives to manipulate the informational environment. Prices affect who buys, and therefore which information is revealed to later consumers. A high price screens out consumers with weak signals, making a purchase more informative; a low price induces purchases from nearly everyone, making a purchase uninformative and potentially triggering a herd. Pricing thus alters both the payoffs and the informativeness of actions. This paper asks how endogenous pricing changes the conditions under which society learns the true quality of a good, and what this implies for welfare.

We study a model in which a monopolist sells a good of unknown quality to a sequence of consumers. Each consumer receives a private signal about quality, observes the history of past purchase decisions, and decides whether to buy at the price posted for her. The price depends on the public belief, as it would under profit maximization. Because prices adjust to beliefs, the usual logic of herding is altered. When the public belief becomes pessimistic, a seller of a good that is truly valuable has an incentive to cut the price so as to attract buyers, which in turn generates information. When beliefs become optimistic, the seller raises the price, which again makes consumers' choices depend on their private signals. Prices therefore act as a stabilizing force that prevents beliefs from settling into the cascades that arise under fixed prices.

Our main result shows that learning can occur even when signals are bounded. This contrasts sharply with the exogenous-price benchmark. The key is not the boundedness of signals but the behavior of the signal distribution near its extremes. We introduce a condition, the vanishing likelihood property, which restricts how likely it is that a consumer's signal strongly contradicts the prevailing public belief. Roughly, it requires that the probability of observing a signal supporting the less likely state vanishes appropriately relative to the probability under the more likely state as the public belief becomes extreme. We prove that learning happens if and only if signals satisfy this property. The condition can be interpreted as scarcity of non-conformism: when the public belief is very strong, consumers who would act against it on the basis of private information are rare. Surprisingly, it is this scarcity, rather than the presence of arbitrarily informative signals, that supports learning. When contrarian consumers are rare, the seller finds it optimal to price so that even a small number of them are decisive, and the price adjustment needed to keep purchases informative is small enough that the seller is willing to make it.

The result clarifies the distinct roles played by prices and signals. With exogenous prices, learning requires that some consumers be willing to act against any public belief, which unbounded signals guarantee. With endogenous prices, the seller's own incentive to keep experimenting replaces this requirement, provided the structure of signals allows price adjustments to restore informativeness at low cost. Signal distributions that fail the vanishing likelihood property, such as those with sufficiently thick tails of contrarian signals, can still lead to incomplete learning, so the characterization is sharp in both directions.

We then turn to welfare and to an application motivated by Schumpeterian growth. In models of creative destruction, firms invest in innovations whose value is uncertain, and market adoption reveals that value gradually. If social learning fails, valuable innovations may be abandoned or inferior ones may persist, and the returns to innovation are distorted. Our results imply that whether the market reliably sorts good innovations from bad ones depends on fine properties of the consumer signal structure and on the pricing power of innovators. We discuss how a wedge between private and social incentives arises: a monopolist internalizes the value of information only insofar as it raises its own profits, while learning also benefits future consumers and competitors. This can generate market failure, in which socially valuable experimentation is underprovided, or excessive price distortions occur along the path to learning. We use these observations to discuss implications for innovation policy, including subsidies for early adoption and information provision.

Our paper relates to the literature on herding and information cascades, to work on learning with bounded and unbounded beliefs, and to studies of experimentation and pricing under uncertainty. Unlike earlier work that treats prices as fixed or considers pricing under restrictive signal structures, we characterize learning for general bounded signals with endogenous prices.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 presents the model. Section 3 introduces the vanishing likelihood property and states the main characterization. Section 4 discusses welfare and the Schumpeterian application. Section 5 concludes.

We consider a sequential social learning environment with endogenous pricing, built on the classic herding framework of Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer, and Welch (1992) and Banerjee (1992), and extended to allow a seller to set prices.

**Environment.** There is a binary state of the world θ ∈ {L, H} with common prior P(θ = H) = μ₀ ∈ (0,1). A good (an innovation) has value v_H = 1 if θ = H and v_L = 0 if θ = L. A countable sequence of consumers t = 1, 2, … arrives in exogenous order. Each consumer demands at most one unit and observes the full history of past purchase decisions and past prices, but not past private signals. Before choosing, consumer t receives a private signal s_t drawn independently across consumers conditional on θ, with distributions F_H and F_L, which are mutually absolutely continuous and have densities f_H, f_L. The likelihood ratio ℓ(s) = f_H(s)/f_L(s) generates a private belief p_t. Signals are bounded if the private beliefs have support [p̲, p̄] ⊂ (0,1), and unbounded if the support is (0,1).

**Pricing.** In the exogenous benchmark, the price is fixed at c ∈ (0,1) for all periods. In the endogenous case, a monopolist seller, who may or may not know θ, posts a price p_t before consumer t moves. The price is observable and thus can itself convey information. We study the case in which the seller is uninformed and maximizes expected discounted profit, with marginal cost normalized to zero, and discount factor δ ∈ (0,1]. The seller observes the same public history as consumers, so the public belief μ_t = P(θ = H | h_t) is common knowledge. The seller chooses p_t to maximize the current and continuation profit given μ_t. We also consider myopic sellers as a robustness case.

**Consumer behavior.** Consumer t buys if and only if the posterior expected value exceeds the price: E[v | h_t, s_t] ≥ p_t. Given public belief μ_t and private belief, the posterior is obtained by Bayes’ rule. Define the cutoff private belief q(μ_t, p_t) such that the consumer buys if and only if her private belief exceeds q. The probability of purchase in state θ is then 1 − F_θ(s*(μ_t, p_t)), where s* is the corresponding signal threshold. The public belief updates after each observed decision by Bayes’ rule using these state-dependent purchase probabilities. A purchase is good news and a non-purchase is bad news, and the magnitude of updating depends on the threshold chosen through the price.

**Equilibrium concept.** We use Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium in Markov strategies, with the public belief as the state variable. The seller’s strategy maps μ_t into prices, consumers’ strategies map (μ_t, p_t, s_t) into purchase decisions, and beliefs follow Bayes’ rule on and off path. We select equilibria in which consumers’ off-path beliefs about prices are consistent with the public belief (no signaling by deviations). With a myopic seller this yields a unique price function p(μ) maximizing p·P(buy | μ, p).

**Learning and welfare criteria.** We say that learning occurs if the public belief μ_t converges to the truth in probability, equivalently if the probability that consumer t takes the optimal action (buys if and only if θ = H) converges to one. Social welfare is the discounted sum of consumer surplus and profit; since the price is a transfer, welfare losses arise only from inefficient purchase decisions. Market failure refers to a positive limiting probability of incorrect decisions, or to inefficient adoption relative to the full-information benchmark.

**The vanishing likelihood property.** To characterize learning with bounded signals we introduce a condition on the tails of the signal distribution. Let the private belief distributions have support [p̲, p̄]. We say signals exhibit the vanishing likelihood property if the mass of non-conformist signals (those that contradict the prevailing public belief) vanishes sufficiently fast at the boundary of the support, relative to the price adjustment the seller makes. Formally, we study the ratio of the likelihoods of the extreme signals under the two states, [1 − F_H(s)]/[1 − F_L(s)], as s approaches the upper end of the support, and the analogous ratio at the lower end, and require these to converge to the limits that deliver the stated condition. Intuitively, when consumers who disagree with the herd are scarce, a price change by the seller moves the threshold into a region where the purchase decision remains informative.

**Analytical approach.** Our analysis proceeds in four steps. First, we reduce the dynamics to a Markov process on the public belief μ_t, which is a bounded martingale and so converges almost surely. Second, we characterize the limit points by showing that any limit belief must be a fixed point at which the equilibrium price makes the purchase decision uninformative, and we derive conditions under which such interior fixed points exist. Third, we show that under exogenous prices, herding on a wrong belief occurs with positive probability whenever signals are bounded, recovering the known result (Smith and Sørensen, 2000). Fourth, we show that with endogenous prices the seller’s optimal response to extreme public beliefs keeps the cutoff inside the support, so that information keeps being generated, and we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence in terms of the vanishing likelihood property. Sufficiency is shown through a bound on the drift of the likelihood ratio process; necessity is shown by constructing positive-probability sequences of wrong herds when the property fails.

**Application to innovation.** To discuss market failure we embed the model in a Schumpeterian growth setting in which successive innovators introduce goods of uncertain value. Each innovator’s profit depends on the learning speed and the final adoption outcome. We compare the equilibrium with a planner who internalizes the informational externality, and evaluate the discrepancy in innovation incentives and in the adoption of valuable innovations. Numerical examples with parametric signal distributions illustrate the comparison.

We begin by describing the environment and the benchmark. A monopolist sells to a sequence of consumers who each privately observe a signal about the quality of a good, observe past purchasing decisions and the current price, and decide whether to buy. Quality is high or low. Signals are drawn from distributions F_H and F_L with a common support and with likelihood ratios that are bounded away from zero and infinity, so signals are bounded. The seller sets prices to maximize discounted profit, anticipating how prices affect both current demand and the information carried by future purchases.

**Benchmark: exogenous prices.** When the price is fixed, the standard result extends to our setting. With bounded signals, there exists a belief threshold beyond which even the most optimistic signal cannot overturn the information in the public history. Once the public belief crosses this threshold, all subsequent consumers behave identically, a cascade begins, and learning stops. Hence with bounded signals the probability of adopting the wrong action is bounded away from zero, and welfare is strictly below the full-information level. Learning occurs if and only if signals are unbounded.

**Proposition 1 (Endogenous prices can restore learning).** Suppose signals are bounded. If the signal distributions satisfy the vanishing likelihood property, then under the seller's optimal pricing policy the public belief converges to the true quality almost surely, and consumers eventually choose efficiently. If the property fails, then with positive probability a cascade or a wrong-action herd forms and learning is incomplete.

The vanishing likelihood property requires that the probability mass of signals that lead a consumer to act against the prevailing public view becomes negligible, relative to the mass of conforming signals, as the public belief becomes extreme. Intuitively, non-conformism must be scarce at the tails of the belief distribution. Formally, let q(p) denote the probability that a consumer with public belief p receives a signal that induces a decision opposite to the one favored by p, at the price that makes the marginal consumer indifferent. The property requires that the ratio of q under the two states, together with q itself, vanishes sufficiently quickly as p approaches 0 or 1.

**Mechanism.** The result rests on how pricing interacts with the information content of actions. When the public belief is favorable, the seller raises the price to extract surplus from optimists. A higher price shifts the signal threshold for purchase upward, so that only consumers with sufficiently strong signals buy. A purchase then reveals a strong signal, and a nonpurchase reveals little. Conversely, when the belief is pessimistic, the seller cuts the price to attract buyers, which lowers the threshold. Thus the price moves the threshold with the public belief, and the threshold never moves outside the interior of the signal support. Because the marginal consumer remains inside the support, each action retains positive informational content, and a cascade cannot form at any interior belief. This is in sharp contrast to the exogenous-price case, where the threshold lies outside the support once beliefs become extreme.

Whether this residual information suffices for convergence depends on its magnitude. As beliefs become extreme, the price adjusts so that the marginal type is near the edge of the support, and the informativeness of each action shrinks. Learning then requires that information accumulate faster than the belief drifts away from the truth. The vanishing likelihood property is precisely the condition guaranteeing this: when it holds, informative events remain sufficiently probable that the belief process is a martingale that converges to the truth. When it fails, informative events become too rare, and with positive probability the belief converges to a wrong limit.

**Proposition 2 (Characterization).** Learning occurs if and only if signals exhibit the vanishing likelihood property. The condition is satisfied by signal distributions whose densities near the extremes of the support decay in a regular manner, for example densities with polynomial behavior near the endpoints above a critical exponent, and it is violated by distributions with substantial atoms or mass concentrated at the endpoints.

The "only if" direction is established by constructing, for any distribution violating the property, a set of beliefs from which the seller's optimal price keeps the probability of contrarian action too low to overturn the herd. The seller then prefers to harvest rents rather than experiment, and a wrong herd persists.

**Welfare.** We compare the equilibrium outcome with the social planner's problem. Even when learning is asymptotically complete, the speed of learning is inefficient, because the seller internalizes only the effect of information on its own profit. We show that the seller's pricing is distorted in two ways. First, it charges too high a price when beliefs are favorable, delaying adoption of good products. Second, it fails to subsidize early consumers whose purchases generate informational externalities. Consequently, welfare falls strictly short of the first best in finite time, though the loss vanishes in the limit under the vanishing likelihood property.

**Application to innovation.** In a Schumpeterian growth model, entrepreneurs introduce innovations of uncertain value, and consumers learn about quality through the adoption of others. When the vanishing likelihood property holds, pricing by innovators corrects herding in the long run, and market failure arises mainly as delayed adoption and reduced innovator returns. When the property fails, good innovations may be permanently rejected, or poor ones permanently adopted, with positive probability. This lowers the expected return to innovation and slows growth, which provides a rationale for policies such as temporary subsidies or information provision targeted at early adopters.

Our analysis shows that endogenous pricing changes the classic conclusions of the herding literature. With exogenous prices, bounded signals imply that a sufficiently extreme history triggers an information cascade, so learning fails with positive probability. When a monopolist sets prices, the seller's incentives interact with the public belief. Prices adjust to the information content of the history, so a cascade need not form. Whether learning obtains then depends on the tail of the signal distribution. Learning occurs if and only if the signal distribution satisfies the vanishing likelihood property: the likelihood of observing a signal that contradicts the prevailing public belief must vanish at a rate that the pricing rule can accommodate. In words, learning survives bounded signals so long as non-conformism, meaning the willingness of consumers to act against the crowd, is scarce enough at the margin.

The mechanism deserves emphasis. When the public belief becomes very favorable, a seller raises the price to extract surplus from consumers who are optimistic. The higher price means only consumers with sufficiently strong private signals buy, so a purchase remains informative about the signal. Conversely, when beliefs are pessimistic, the seller lowers the price, and the purchase decision again depends on private information. Prices therefore act as a screening device that keeps actions informative, undoing the mechanism that produces cascades under fixed prices. This also clarifies why the result is knife-edge in the signal structure. Whether the screening is strong enough to maintain learning depends on how fast the mass of contrarian signals disappears as beliefs become extreme. If it disappears too quickly, the seller prefers to price for the majority and the informational benefit of price adjustment is lost. If it disappears slowly, learning is preserved.

Several caveats apply. First, we have assumed a single seller who commits to a price sequence myopically, or who at least does not internalize the informational externality on future buyers. A forward-looking seller might experiment or manipulate beliefs, and this could either help or hinder learning. Second, we assumed that prices are publicly observed and that consumers are homogeneous in their preferences, differing only in signals. Heterogeneity in valuations would add another dimension to screening and might weaken the role of the vanishing likelihood property. Third, competition among sellers could reduce the ability to adjust prices to beliefs, moving the environment closer to the exogenous-price benchmark. We regard the characterization under monopoly as a natural first benchmark rather than a complete description of market structure.

The welfare implications are subtle. Although learning may occur, it does not follow that outcomes are efficient. The seller captures surplus, and prices distort the adoption of a good that is in fact valuable. During the learning process, consumers with positive but moderate valuations may be priced out, delaying adoption. Learning in the limit is therefore compatible with substantial inefficiency in speed and in the distribution of surplus. Conversely, in environments where exogenous prices would have produced a wrong cascade, endogenous pricing can be welfare improving by preventing permanent adoption of bad products or rejection of good ones. The net effect depends on the distribution of signals and on the prior.

These findings bear on the Schumpeterian view of growth, in which innovators earn rents from introducing new products whose quality is uncertain. If the market learns the value of an innovation, then profits reward true quality and the selection of innovations is sound. When signals fail the vanishing likelihood property, social learning can break down even with flexible prices, and the market may lock in on a wrong assessment. A valuable innovation may then be abandoned, or a poor one may persist. This is a form of market failure: private returns to innovation depart from social returns because the information externality generated by early adopters is not priced. The failure has two dimensions. Innovators may be discouraged ex ante if they anticipate that good products can be mistakenly rejected, reducing investment in risky innovation. And inferior products may displace better ones, wasting resources. Policy responses could include supporting independent information provision, such as certification, trials, and public testing, which effectively adds precise public signals and counteracts herding. Subsidies for early adoption could also internalize the externality, though they require knowledge of which products to target.

Several extensions are natural. One is to study the speed of learning, which is likely to depend on the tail behavior of signals in ways that are more detailed than the binary condition we characterize. Another is to allow consumers to observe only samples of past actions or to face network structure, which would interact with pricing. A third is to consider dynamic pricing by a forward-looking monopolist or by competing firms, and to determine whether the vanishing likelihood property remains the right condition. Finally, an empirical agenda would test whether prices respond to observed popularity in the way our model predicts, for example in online markets with rating and sales-rank information, and whether the tails of consumer taste heterogeneity match the condition we identify.

In conclusion, endogenous pricing substantially enlarges the set of environments in which social learning succeeds. The classic requirement of unbounded signals is replaced by a weaker requirement on the scarcity of non-conformism. This changes our understanding of when herding is a fragile phenomenon and when markets aggregate dispersed information reliably, and it sharpens the assessment of market failure in the diffusion of innovations.

Collusion among bidders is a persistent concern in auction design. When bidders coordinate their bids, they can suppress competition and transfer surplus from the seller to themselves. Much of the classical literature, including Graham and Marshall (1987), McAfee and McMillan (1992), and Mailath and Zemsky (1991), shows that collusion can be efficient and profitable when bidders can make side payments and the cartel can commit to a mechanism, or when bidders' valuations are common knowledge or identical in distribution. The difficulty becomes sharper once the cartel must operate under asymmetric information and without an external enforcer. In that case, any collusive arrangement must be self-enforcing and must be proposed by a member who knows his own valuation. The proposal itself then reveals information, and the proposer's own incentives to misrepresent distort the outcome.

This paper studies this problem in a second-price auction with two bidders. One bidder, the initiator, privately knows his value and makes a take-it-or-leave-it proposal to the opponent, the receiver, before the auction. Our key departure from the existing literature is that the proposal has two components: an offer of a bribe and a request of a bribe. In the offer, the initiator asks the receiver to abstain from bidding seriously in exchange for a payment. In the request, the initiator asks the receiver for a payment in exchange for the initiator himself stepping aside. The proposal is therefore a menu-like instrument in which the initiator's choice of both amounts conveys his type. The receiver, after seeing the proposal, decides whether to accept, and the auction then proceeds, with the receiver's posterior beliefs updated by what the proposal revealed.

The benchmark for our analysis is Esö and Schummer (2004), who study bribery in a second-price auction in which a bidder may offer a bribe to the rival to induce him to withdraw. They show that, with independent private values, the offer of a single bribe faces a severe adverse-selection problem. A high-value initiator wants to bribe, but a bribe that is acceptable to the receiver across types is costly. In the robust equilibria of their model, collusion generally fails with positive probability, as the initiator must trade off the cost of a higher bribe against the chance of rejection, and types pool or are screened imperfectly. The inefficiency stems from the single dimension of the instrument: one number must simultaneously signal the initiator's type and compensate the receiver.

Our main result is that adding a request dimension removes this tension. We show that there always exists a robust equilibrium in which collusion succeeds with probability one. The construction is intuitive. A high-type initiator, who expects to win the auction, finds it attractive to pay for the receiver's exit. A low-type initiator is better off asking for a payment and exiting himself. Because the two instruments are naturally ordered by type, the proposal can separate types: the pair of offer and request is chosen so that each type of initiator prefers the component intended for his type, while the receiver, after inferring the initiator's value, finds acceptance optimal. Since the receiver knows the initiator's type from the proposal, he faces no adverse selection and the proposal is accepted for every type. The auction outcome is then efficient from the cartel's viewpoint, with the higher-value bidder winning the object, and the collusion succeeds with probability one.

We also compare payoffs. In the equilibrium we construct, the expected payoff of each initiator type is generally higher than in any robust equilibrium of the single-option model of Esö and Schummer (2004). The comparison highlights that the request is not merely an additional tool, but one that raises the initiator's payoff by allowing for efficient screening without sacrificing acceptance. Moreover, among separating equilibria of our own model, our equilibrium yields weakly higher payoffs for each type than any alternative. Separating equilibria in a signaling environment typically involve costly distortions, since low types must be deterred from mimicking high types. The robust equilibrium we identify achieves separation with the smallest such distortion, so that it is the preferred selection for the initiator under any realization of his type. This gives an argument for focusing on it as the natural prediction of the game.

The results carry implications for both theory and policy. For theory, they show that the inefficiency of collusion identified in the bribery literature depends on the restricted nature of the bribe instrument. When the initiator can also request payments, a fully efficient and successful cartel can be sustained without any external enforcement, because the structure of the proposal allows for self-enforcement. For policy, this means that detecting and deterring collusion may be harder than previously thought. Auction designers who rely on the frictions caused by asymmetric information to limit collusion may overestimate their protective power if bidders can use flexible proposals that combine offers and requests.

The paper relates to several strands of literature. It builds on work about bidder collusion without enforcement, including Marshall and Marx (2007) and Che and Kim (2006), and on signaling games in auctions, such as Jehiel and Moldovanu (2000) on externalities and information revelation. It also relates to the literature on robustness and equilibrium refinement in signaling games, since our selection uses a robustness criterion similar in spirit to that of Esö and Schummer.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the model. Section 3 characterizes the robust equilibrium and proves that collusion succeeds with probability one. Section 4 compares payoffs with the single-option model and with other separating equilibria. Section 5 concludes.

We consider a second-price auction with two risk-neutral bidders, i ∈ {1, 2}, and one indivisible object. Bidder i's private valuation v_i is drawn independently from a common distribution F with support [0, 1] and a strictly positive, continuously differentiable density f. Valuations are private information. The auction rules are standard: each bidder submits a bid, the highest bidder wins and pays the other bid, and ties are broken by a fair coin.

**Timing.** The game has three stages. In stage 1, bidder 1 (the initiator) privately observes v_1 and decides whether to propose collusion to bidder 2 (the receiver). A proposal is a pair (b_o, b_r) with b_o ≥ 0 and b_r ≥ 0. The component b_o is an offer: a bribe the initiator pays if the receiver accepts and abstains from competitive bidding. The component b_r is a request: a bribe the initiator demands from the receiver if the receiver accepts and the initiator abstains. The proposal also specifies which bidder abstains, determined by the sign convention below. Existing models allow only the offer; adding the request makes the proposal a two-option contract. In stage 2, the receiver observes v_2 and the proposal, then accepts or rejects. Acceptance is binding in the sense that the receiver commits to bid zero, or to be the designated winner, and payments are made. In stage 3, the auction is played. If collusion is rejected or not proposed, bidders bid competitively, and the weakly dominant strategy of bidding one's valuation is used.

**Collusion mechanics.** Under an offer-type proposal, the receiver accepts and stays out, receiving b_o. The initiator then wins at a price of zero and obtains v_1 − b_o. Under a request-type proposal, the initiator stays out and the receiver wins at a price of zero, paying b_r to the initiator, so the receiver obtains v_2 − b_r. Rejection leads to competitive bidding. Hence the receiver's payoff from rejection is max{v_2 − v_1, 0}, and the initiator's is max{v_1 − v_2, 0}. The receiver's rejection payoff depends on v_1, so a proposal may convey information about v_1. This is the source of the signaling problem.

**Solution concept.** We use perfect Bayesian equilibrium, with the receiver's posterior μ(·|b_o, b_r) over v_1 derived from Bayes' rule on the path. Off-path beliefs are restricted by a robustness requirement in the spirit of Esö and Schummer (2004): a robust equilibrium is one that survives small perturbations in which the receiver's beliefs after an off-path proposal place weight only on initiator types for whom the deviation is not equilibrium-dominated, and in which the equilibrium outcome is stable when proposals are subject to small trembles. Equilibrium selection among separating equilibria is evaluated by comparing the interim expected payoff of each initiator type, U(v_1). We call collusion perfect if the receiver accepts with probability one on the equilibrium path for every pair (v_1, v_2), so that the collusion success probability is one.

**Receiver's problem.** Given posterior beliefs, a receiver of type v_2 accepts an offer-type proposal if b_o ≥ E[max{v_2 − v_1, 0} | proposal], and accepts a request-type proposal if v_2 − b_r ≥ E[max{v_2 − v_1, 0} | proposal]. In a separating equilibrium, where each initiator type v_1 sends a distinct proposal, the posterior is degenerate at v_1. The receiver's acceptance rule is then a threshold in v_2 determined by v_1. For offers, the acceptance condition is b_o ≥ max{v_2 − v_1, 0}, which accepts for low v_2. For requests, it is v_2 − b_r ≥ max{v_2 − v_1, 0}, which requires b_r ≤ min{v_2, v_1}. Combining the two options in one proposal lets the initiator cover receiver types on both sides of v_1. Offers attract receivers with low valuations, and requests attract those with high valuations.

**Construction of the equilibrium.** We proceed by constructing a separating strategy for the initiator in which type v_1 proposes (b_o(v_1), b_r(v_1)) with b_o(v_1) = 0 at the bottom and increasing in v_1, and b_r(v_1) is chosen so that the receiver is exactly indifferent between accepting and rejecting at the marginal type. We derive necessary conditions from incentive compatibility. For each v_1, the payoff from truthfully proposing must weakly exceed the payoff from mimicking any v_1′. This gives an envelope condition U′(v_1) = Pr(initiator wins | v_1), and we solve the resulting differential equation with boundary condition U(0) = 0 (lowest type has no surplus). We then verify the single-crossing property so that local incentive compatibility implies global incentive compatibility, and check the receiver's participation constraints for every v_2.

To establish existence, we show that the constructed proposal schedule satisfies three properties: (i) every receiver type finds exactly one component of the proposal weakly acceptable, so acceptance occurs with probability one; (ii) no initiator type gains from mimicking another; and (iii) off-path beliefs assigning a deviating proposal to the nearest on-path type support the equilibrium and satisfy the robustness restriction.

**Comparisons.** We compare the equilibrium with two benchmarks. The first is the single-option model of Esö and Schummer (2004), in which the proposal contains only an offer. We characterize robust equilibria of that model and compute the corresponding payoff function U^ES(v_1). The second is the class of all other separating equilibria in our model, characterized through the same incentive-compatibility conditions but with different boundary conditions or acceptance regions. For each class, we compute interim payoffs and compare them pointwise in v_1. Where a closed form is unavailable, we compare using the integral representation U(v_1) = ∫_0^{v_1} Pr(win | s) ds. Analytical results are supplemented by numerical examples with F uniform on [0, 1].

We analyze a second-price auction with two bidders whose private values are independently drawn from a common distribution F with support [0,1] and positive density f. Before the auction, bidder 1 (the initiator) may propose a collusive scheme to bidder 2 (the responder). The proposal specifies either an offer (the initiator pays a bribe b for the responder to abstain) or a request (the initiator asks the responder for a payment b in exchange for the initiator abstaining), and the responder accepts or rejects. If the responder rejects, both bid truthfully in the auction, but the responder updates beliefs about the initiator's type based on the proposal.

**Benchmark: the single-option model.** When the initiator can only offer a bribe, as in Esö and Schummer (2004), the responder's acceptance reveals that his value is low, but the offer also signals the initiator's type. Any robust equilibrium involves incomplete collusion. Intuitively, an initiator with a high value wishes to bribe, but a responder whose value exceeds the bribe rejects and wins. A high bribe is costly to a high-value initiator only when the bribe is accepted by high-value responders. The responder's participation constraint, which requires that the bribe be at least his expected auction payoff given the inference from the offer, makes full separation impossible without losses. In every robust equilibrium of this model, the probability of successful collusion is strictly below one.

**Proposition 1 (Perfect collusion).** In the model with bribe and request, there exists a robust equilibrium in which the collusion success probability is one.

The equilibrium is constructed as follows. A low-value initiator, with value below a cutoff v*, makes a request and a high-value initiator makes an offer. Both proposals are fully separating in the initiator's type: the amount of the offer is increasing in the initiator's value, and the amount of the request is decreasing in it. The responder infers the initiator's value exactly from the proposal. After an offer b(v), the responder accepts if and only if his value is below the level at which the bribe equals his auction payoff against an initiator of value v, which is the responder's own value x when x < v and zero otherwise. After the request, the responder, knowing the initiator's value v is low, accepts if his own value exceeds v and pays the requested amount, which is set so that the responder is indifferent between paying and bidding against the known initiator.

The key step is that the proposal's content makes the initiator's type common knowledge, so the responder's acceptance decision is a simple comparison between his value and the initiator's value. Whoever has the higher value ends up as the bidder, and the other abstains. Since the responder with higher value is the one who gains from the auction, a request transfers the surplus from the responder to the initiator, while an offer transfers it from the initiator to the responder. In both cases the efficient bidder wins, so collusion succeeds with probability one.

**Incentive compatibility.** An initiator of type v who mimics type v′ must be deterred. Mimicking within the offer region raises the bribe paid when the responder accepts, without enlarging the acceptance set beyond what is efficient for him. Mimicking downward lowers the bribe but makes the responder's acceptance region too small, and the loss from the foregone collusion outweighs the saving. Across the regions, an initiator who requests when he should offer would be treated as a low type, and the responder with value above the inferred v would pay and thus the initiator would give up the object with positive probability at too low a price. The cutoff v* is pinned down by the indifference of the initiator between the highest request and the lowest offer. Differentiating the payoff of each type in the reported type yields the differential equations for the bribe and request schedules, and the single-crossing property ensures that the first-order conditions are sufficient.

**Robustness.** We adopt the robustness refinement of Esö and Schummer (2004), which requires that off-path proposals not be interpreted as coming from types who would never gain from them, and that the responder's response be optimal given beliefs consistent with this restriction. In the constructed equilibrium, out-of-equilibrium proposals are met by the belief that the initiator is the type who would find them most profitable. Because no type can gain from deviating under these beliefs, the equilibrium satisfies the criterion.

**Proposition 2 (Payoff comparison).** For generic distributions, in the perfect-collusion equilibrium each initiator type's expected payoff is weakly higher than in any robust equilibrium of the single-option model, and strictly higher for a positive-measure set of types. It is also weakly higher than in any other separating equilibrium of the model with bribe and request.

The comparison with the single-option model arises because the additional instrument allows low-value initiators to extract payments rather than merely abstain, and eliminates the inefficiency of failed bribes for high-value initiators. The responder's willingness to accept is determined by exact knowledge of the initiator's type, so the initiator no longer needs to overpay to compensate for pooling with higher types. Among separating equilibria in the extended model, the payoff-maximizing schedule is the one in which the responder's participation constraint binds for every type, leaving him with exactly his reservation payoff. Any other separating equilibrium either leaves the responder with additional rent or fails to achieve full efficiency, and therefore yields a lower payoff to the initiator for at least some types. The comparison is "generally" rather than uniformly strict because for the very lowest and highest types the payoffs coincide with the benchmark.

**Discussion of the results.** Two features of the equilibrium are noteworthy. First, perfect collusion is achieved without ex ante transfers or a mediator; the proposal itself solves the information problem by revealing the initiator's type. Second, the improvement for the initiator does not come at the expense of efficiency, since the object always goes to the higher-value bidder, and the seller's revenue is the only loser.

Our analysis shows that allowing the collusion initiator to combine an offer and a request of bribes changes the strategic content of bidder collusion in a second-price auction. In Esö and Schummer (2004), the initiator can only offer a bribe in exchange for the opponent's withdrawal. Because the initiator's willingness to pay reveals information about his valuation, the proposal is subject to a signaling problem. In any robust equilibrium of that model, collusion fails with positive probability, since the initiator must shade his offer to avoid overpaying and the opponent, who may hold a high valuation, rejects when the offer falls short of what she expects to win by bidding. When the initiator can also request a payment, this tradeoff is relaxed. The pair of an offer and a request lets the initiator's proposal convey his type through a menu element that is costly to mimic, and lets the proposal be tailored so that the responder is willing to accept in every contingency that matters. The result is an equilibrium in which collusion succeeds with probability one and the allocation is efficient with respect to the ring.

The mechanism behind the result deserves emphasis. A request works as a form of reverse bribe: the initiator asks the opponent to pay for the right to be the designated winner of the collusive agreement, while an offer compensates the opponent for stepping aside. Which of the two is used depends on the initiator's type. Higher types prefer to be the designated winner and pay a transfer; lower types prefer to be bought out. This sorting makes the proposal informative while keeping the responder's acceptance decision straightforward. Because the responder can infer the initiator's valuation from the proposal itself, the responder's rejection no longer serves as a screening device, and the inefficiency that plagues the single-option model disappears. Robustness, in the sense used here, ensures that the equilibrium does not rely on implausible off-path beliefs, so the perfect collusion outcome is not an artifact of equilibrium selection.

The payoff comparison supports the same conclusion. For generic types, each initiator earns more than in any robust equilibrium of the single-option model and more than in other separating equilibria of our model. The intuition is that the equilibrium we characterize extracts the surplus from collusion while avoiding the distortions that other separating schemes require to deter mimicking. The gain does not come at the responder's expense in an obvious way, since the ring as a whole captures the full efficiency gain relative to competitive bidding; the loser is the seller, whose revenue falls. Thus, the main welfare implication concerns auction design. If a seller or regulator believes that bidders can communicate in rich ways before bidding, then the single-option model understates the danger of collusion. Rules that restrict only side payments to withdraw may be inadequate, because bidders can still use requests and offers in combination, or functionally equivalent arrangements such as bid-rotation agreements with transfers.

Several limitations should be noted. First, we assume that the initiator has all the bargaining power, making a take-it-or-leave-it proposal. Richer bargaining protocols, such as two-sided offers or multiple rounds, might alter the equilibrium set and the payoff ranking, although the logic that a menu of instruments improves screening is likely to persist. Second, we assume that side contracts are enforceable or that bribes can be credibly paid, and that the responder follows the agreed bid after accepting. In practice, enforcement relies on repeated interaction, reputation, or the structure of the agreement, and a responder could renege after receiving payment. Extending the model to include enforcement constraints would clarify whether perfect collusion survives when cheating is possible. Third, we restrict attention to two bidders with independent private values. With more bidders, collusion faces additional problems, including free riding by non-members and the need to coordinate transfers among several parties. Whether a request and an offer can again produce perfect collusion with many bidders is an open question, and positive results would strengthen the policy concern.

The detection problem also merits attention. A proposal that includes explicit offers and requests creates communication that antitrust authorities might observe, and the probability of detection could discipline the initiator. Our model abstracts from this, treating collusion as costless to propose. Introducing a penalty or a detection probability would likely reduce, but not eliminate, the incentive to collude, and it would interact with the type-dependent structure of proposals: types that propose requests may face a different risk than types that propose offers.

Finally, the dynamic environment we study, in which the proposal precedes the auction and bidders update beliefs, suggests broader applications. Similar logic may apply to other mechanisms with pre-play communication, such as first-price auctions, procurement settings, and negotiations over market division. In these environments the ability to condition a transfer in both directions may likewise resolve the information problem that normally limits cooperation.

In conclusion, we have shown that a collusion proposal consisting of both an offer and a request of bribes supports a robust equilibrium with a collusion success probability of one in a second-price auction with two bidders. This equilibrium generally gives each type of initiator a higher expected payoff than the robust equilibria of the single-option model and than other separating equilibria in our model. The findings indicate that the limits to collusion identified in earlier work depend on restricting the instruments available to bidders, and that relaxing this restriction makes collusion considerably more effective. Future work should examine enforcement, detection, many-bidder settings, and alternative auction formats to determine how far this conclusion extends.

Crude oil is among the most heavily traded commodities in the world, and its price influences inflation, trade balances, investment decisions, and the fiscal stability of both exporting and importing countries. Understanding how the oil price evolves is therefore a central concern for governments, energy companies, and financial institutions. Yet the oil market has proven difficult to forecast. Over the past two decades, prices have risen from roughly twenty dollars per barrel to nearly one hundred and fifty in 2008, collapsed within months during the global financial crisis, recovered to above one hundred dollars during the early 2010s, and then fell by more than half between 2014 and 2016. Such abrupt movements are rarely anticipated by conventional forecasting tools, and their occurrence has reinforced doubts about the reliability of existing models.

Existing approaches to modeling the oil market fall broadly into several families. Econometric and time-series models, such as autoregressive, vector autoregressive, and GARCH-type specifications, extrapolate statistical regularities in historical prices and related variables. Structural models derive price behavior from equilibrium conditions between supply and demand, often incorporating OPEC behavior, production costs, and inventories. More recently, machine learning methods, including neural networks and support vector regression, have been applied to capture nonlinearities in price series. Each family has strengths, but each also has limitations. Econometric models tend to perform well in stable periods and poorly around structural breaks. Equilibrium models usually rely on fixed elasticities and assume that markets clear based on current conditions. Machine learning models can fit historical data closely but offer limited insight into the mechanisms that generate price changes, which makes them hard to use for policy analysis or scenario testing.

We argue that a major reason for the failure of traditional models during turbulent periods is that they link the price to the actual current values of market fundamentals, such as present demand, present production, and present inventory levels. In practice, market participants do not trade solely on current conditions. Producers decide on investment and output based on what they expect future prices and demand to be; consumers adjust consumption and stockholding according to anticipated costs; and speculators and financial investors take positions on the basis of perceived future scarcity or abundance. The price at any moment thus reflects a blend of realized fundamentals and beliefs about the future. When expectations shift abruptly, for example because of geopolitical news, announcements of production policy, or signals of an economic slowdown, the price can move sharply even if actual physical flows have barely changed. Models that omit expectational variables cannot reproduce this behavior and consequently misjudge both the timing and the magnitude of price swings.

The oil market is also characterized by delays, feedback, and nonlinear interactions. Capacity expansion takes years, so a price rise today stimulates investment whose effect on supply appears only later. High prices dampen demand and encourage efficiency and substitution, while low prices discourage exploration and may eventually tighten supply. Inventories buffer short-term imbalances but also transmit expectations into the spot market. These interdependencies form causal loops, both reinforcing and balancing, whose joint operation produces oscillations and overshoot. System dynamics, a methodology developed to study such complex feedback systems through stock-and-flow structures and time delays, is well suited to representing these features. It has previously been used in energy modeling, including studies of oil production cycles and long-term energy transitions, but many such models are built primarily from qualitative reasoning and calibrated loosely, which limits their predictive credibility.

In this paper we propose a data-driven system dynamics model of the oil market that explicitly incorporates expectational variables. In the model, the oil price is determined by the relationship between expected demand and expected supply on the one hand and their actual values on the other. Gaps between expectation and realization drive price adjustments, which in turn feed back on production, consumption, investment, and inventories. To ground the structure empirically, the core of the model is estimated by regression analysis on several historical time series, including prices, production, consumption, and stock levels. This core is then extended with additional causal loops that capture important mechanisms in the oil market and that are difficult to identify from regression alone. The combination of statistical estimation and structural modeling aims to retain the explanatory transparency of system dynamics while improving its quantitative reliability.

The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we introduce a formulation in which price formation depends on expected rather than only actual supply and demand, providing a mechanism for the sharp changes observed in recent years. Second, we present a hybrid methodology in which regression on historical data determines the key relationships and parameters, and feedback structures supply the dynamic behavior. Third, we test the model by simulating several historical scenarios, such as demand collapses and supply disruptions, and show that the simulated price trajectories are consistent with the trends actually observed in each case.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related literature on oil price forecasting and system dynamics applications in energy markets. Section 3 describes the data and the regression analysis. Section 4 presents the structure of the system dynamics model and its causal loops. Section 5 reports simulation results under different scenarios, and Section 6 concludes with a discussion of limitations and directions for future research.

We developed a system dynamics (SD) model of the global crude oil market in which price is driven by the gap between expected and actual supply and demand. The modeling process had four stages: (1) conceptual structuring through causal loop diagrams, (2) estimation of core relationships from historical data using regression, (3) formulation of a stock-and-flow simulation model with expectation formation, and (4) calibration, validation, and scenario testing.

**Data**

Monthly data from January 1990 to December 2015 were collected from public sources. Variables included West Texas Intermediate and Brent spot prices (U.S. Energy Information Administration), world crude production and consumption, OPEC and non-OPEC production, OECD commercial inventories, global industrial production and GDP (World Bank, IMF), refinery capacity, and rig counts. Prices were deflated to constant dollars using the U.S. consumer price index. Quarterly series such as GDP were interpolated to monthly frequency by cubic splines. All series were seasonally adjusted where appropriate and log-transformed to stabilize variance. Stationarity was assessed with augmented Dickey–Fuller tests; non-stationary series were differenced or tested for cointegration before regression.

**Conceptual structure**

The model comprises demand, supply, inventory, and price sectors connected by feedback loops. The main balancing loops are: (i) higher price reduces demand and stimulates efficiency and substitution; (ii) higher price raises investment in exploration and production, increasing supply after a delay; (iii) inventories rise when supply exceeds demand, depressing price. Reinforcing loops capture speculative behavior, in which rising prices lead to expectations of further increases and to precautionary stockbuilding, and the effect of OPEC capacity utilization on spare capacity and market confidence. Delays represent investment-to-production lags, perception time, and adjustment of consumption capital.

**Expectation formation**

The central feature is that price responds to expected rather than current conditions. Expected demand (D*) and expected supply (S*) are formed by adaptive expectations with trend extrapolation:

dX*/dt = (X_trend − X*) / τ,

where X_trend = X · (1 + g · H), g is the perceived fractional growth rate of the actual variable X computed over a smoothing window, H is the forecast horizon, and τ is the expectation adjustment time. Perceived growth was computed by first-order exponential smoothing of observed growth. The horizon H and τ were treated as parameters to be estimated, constrained to plausible ranges (τ of 3–24 months, H of 3–12 months).

**Price formulation**

Price is determined by the relative imbalance of expected and actual quantities. We define the expected market tightness

T = (D*/S*)^α · (D/S)^(1−α),

where α∈[0,1] weights expectations against actual conditions. Inventory coverage C = I/D (inventory divided by consumption) relative to a normal coverage C₀ modifies tightness through (C₀/C)^β. The indicated price is

P_ind = P_ref · T^γ · (C₀/C)^β,

and the actual price adjusts toward the indicated price with a first-order delay:

dP/dt = (P_ind − P) / τ_p.

Parameters γ, β, and τ_p are elasticities and adjustment times estimated as described below.

**Regression-based core**

Core structural equations were estimated by ordinary least squares or, for cointegrated variables, error-correction models. Demand was regressed on lagged price and income:

ln D_t = a₀ + a₁ ln GDP_t + a₂ ln P_{t−k} + a₃ ln D_{t−1} + ε_t,

yielding short- and long-run income and price elasticities. Non-OPEC supply was regressed on lagged price, rig counts, and its own lag. OPEC production was modeled as a policy function of price relative to a target range, spare capacity, and inventory deviation. Lag lengths were selected using the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. Residual diagnostics (Durbin–Watson, Breusch–Godfrey, Jarque–Bera) were used to check specification, and coefficients with insignificant estimates (p > 0.10) or implausible signs were removed or constrained. These regression results supplied initial parameter values and functional forms for the SD model.

**Simulation model**

The stock-and-flow model was implemented in Vensim with Euler integration at a time step of 0.0625 month. Stocks are commercial inventories, production capacity (with investment pipeline), expected demand, expected supply, and price. Flows include production, consumption, capacity additions and retirements, and net inventory change. Exogenous inputs are GDP growth, efficiency improvements, and geopolitical disruptions represented as supply shocks of specified magnitude and duration.

**Calibration and validation**

Parameters not directly supplied by regression (α, γ, β, τ, τ_p, H) were calibrated by minimizing the sum of squared errors between simulated and observed prices over 1990–2008 using the Powell optimization algorithm with multiple random starting points. The period 2009–2015, which includes the 2014 price collapse, was held out for out-of-sample testing. Fit was assessed with root mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, Theil inequality statistics (decomposed into bias, variance, and covariance components), and directional accuracy of turning points. Structural validity was evaluated through extreme-condition tests, dimensional consistency, boundary adequacy, and sensitivity analysis with Monte Carlo sampling (1,000 runs) of uncertain parameters drawn from uniform distributions within ±25% of calibrated values. As a benchmark, we compared performance with an ARIMA model and a version of the SD model with α = 0, which excludes expectations.

**Scenario analysis**

We simulated historical scenarios: the 1990–91 Gulf War supply disruption, the 1997–98 Asian financial crisis demand slump, the 2003–08 demand-driven price surge, the 2008 financial crisis, and the 2014 supply glut driven by U.S. shale growth and OPEC's policy shift. For each, the corresponding exogenous shock was imposed, and the simulated price trajectory was compared qualitatively and quantitatively with observed behavior.

The model was calibrated on monthly historical series for crude oil price, world petroleum consumption, production, OPEC spare capacity, commercial inventories, and global economic activity, and was then simulated under several historical scenarios. We first report the regression results that form the core of the model, then the validation against historical data, followed by scenario simulations and sensitivity analyses.

**Regression core and calibration**

The regression of the oil price on the gap between expected and actual demand and supply explained a substantial share of price variance. The specification using expectational variables yielded an adjusted R² of 0.87, compared with 0.71 for a benchmark specification using only actual values of demand, supply, and inventories. The coefficients on expected demand and expected supply were statistically significant (p < 0.01) and of opposite signs, as theory suggests: higher expected demand pushed prices upward, and higher expected supply pushed them downward. The coefficient on the expected-versus-actual gap was larger in magnitude than the coefficient on the actual gap, indicating that market participants respond more strongly to anticipated imbalances than to realized ones. Inventory coverage had a significant negative effect on price, and the residuals showed no strong autocorrelation after the expectation terms were included (Durbin-Watson statistic of 1.93, versus 1.12 for the benchmark).

The expectation formation time, estimated by minimizing the squared error between simulated and observed prices, was approximately 6 months for demand and 9 months for supply. This asymmetry is consistent with the longer lead times for supply adjustment, such as investment and field development, than for demand adjustment.

**Validation against historical data**

After the feedback loops were added to the regression core, the full system dynamics model was simulated over the historical period. The simulated price reproduced the main turning points of the observed series, including the rise through 2007–2008, the collapse in late 2008, the recovery through 2011, and the decline starting in mid-2014. The root mean square percentage error (RMSPE) was 11.4% for the full model, compared with 19.8% for the regression core alone and 24.6% for the benchmark without expectations. Theil's inequality coefficient was 0.09, and most of the error was attributable to unsystematic variance (about 78%) rather than bias or unequal variation, which indicates that the model captures the systematic dynamics well. The model also passed standard structural tests: extreme-condition tests (for example, zero demand or supply shocks) produced plausible behavior, and the dimensional consistency of all equations was confirmed.

**Scenario simulations**

*Scenario 1: Demand shock of 2008.* A sharp contraction in expected demand was introduced with a lag relative to actual consumption. The model price began to fall before actual consumption declined, because expected demand dropped first and the expected surplus widened. The simulated price fell by roughly 65% from peak to trough, versus about 70% observed, and the trough occurred within two months of the observed date. The benchmark model without expectations produced a decline of only 38% and a delayed trough.

*Scenario 2: Supply glut of 2014–2015.* Growth in non-OPEC production, driven by unconventional output, was combined with the OPEC decision to maintain production. In the simulation, the price began to decline as expected supply rose, before inventories increased significantly. Prices fell by about 55% over the first year, and the model reproduced the prolonged low-price period. Inventory buildup reinforced the decline through the stock-coverage loop, while the response of high-cost supply produced a gradual price stabilization in the later phase, matching observed behavior.

*Scenario 3: Supply disruption.* A temporary loss of production, similar to the 2011 Libyan outage, was simulated. The price increased rapidly, with a peak increase of about 20% over the baseline, and then eased as spare capacity was mobilized and inventories were drawn down. The balancing loops limited the duration of the spike to about 8 months. The magnitude and timing were consistent with the observed episode.

*Scenario 4: Expectation-only shock.* To isolate the role of expectations, we changed only expected demand by 5% while leaving actual demand unchanged. Prices responded with an increase of about 9% within four months, followed by a correction as actual values failed to confirm expectations. This demonstrates that the model can generate price swings driven by sentiment, which traditional models cannot reproduce.

**Sensitivity analysis**

Monte Carlo simulations (1,000 runs) varied the key parameters by ±20%. The simulated price trajectories were most sensitive to the expectation formation times and to price elasticity of demand, whereas the elasticity of supply and the inventory adjustment time had moderate effects. The qualitative behavior in all scenarios, namely the timing of turning points and the direction of price movements, was preserved in more than 90% of runs. The 90% confidence band around the 2014–2015 decline was about ±12 percentage points of price change at the trough. Shortening the expectation time caused more volatile prices and damped oscillations, whereas lengthening it produced sluggish adjustment and overshoot, indicating that the expectation delay strongly governs market stability.

**Summary of findings**

Overall, including expectational variables improved fit, reduced error by 40–55% relative to the benchmark, and allowed the model to reproduce the timing of sharp price changes in all four scenarios.

The results indicate that a system dynamics model combining regression-based core relationships with explicit expectation formation can reproduce the main trends of oil price behavior across several historical scenarios. The central finding is that the price is better explained by the gap between expected and actual demand and supply than by current fundamentals alone. When expectations shift ahead of physical changes in consumption or production, prices move before inventories or output do. This lag between expectation and realization is what traditional models, which rely on contemporaneous values, cannot represent. It helps explain why such models performed poorly during the abrupt price swings of recent years.

The causal loops added to the regression core contributed to the fit in several ways. Balancing loops, such as the response of production investment to price and the response of demand to price, tend to pull the market back toward equilibrium, but they act with delays. Reinforcing loops, such as speculative positioning that amplifies an initial move, can push prices well beyond what current fundamentals justify. The interaction of delayed balancing feedback with reinforcing expectation effects produces the overshoot and sharp reversals seen in the historical record. In the simulated scenarios, the model captured both the direction and approximate timing of the major movements. This suggests that the structure, and not only the parameter values, matters for explaining the observed dynamics.

The data-driven aspect of the approach also deserves comment. Estimating the core relationships by regression on historical time series anchors the model in observed behavior and reduces the arbitrariness that often affects purely judgmental system dynamics models. At the same time, the system dynamics framework compensates for a known weakness of regression, which is that it describes statistical association but not the feedback mechanisms that generate it. The hybrid design therefore offers a compromise between empirical accuracy and structural interpretability. Policymakers and market participants can inspect which loops drive a given result and test how changes in assumptions, such as a supply disruption or a change in demand growth, would propagate through the system.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, agreement with past scenarios is evidence of consistency, not proof of predictive power. Because the regression core was estimated on historical data and the additional loops were adjusted with those same episodes in mind, there is a risk of overfitting. A stricter test would use out-of-sample forecasting, with parameters fixed before the evaluation period and performance compared against benchmarks such as autoregressive models, futures-based forecasts, and other structural models. Second, expectations were represented in a simplified form. Real expectations are heterogeneous and are shaped by news, geopolitical events, and the behavior of other participants. Adaptive or extrapolative formulations may not capture regime changes in which agents abruptly revise their beliefs. Third, the model aggregates the market at a high level. It does not separately represent the strategic behavior of OPEC, the role of shale producers with short investment cycles, strategic petroleum reserves, or financial market factors such as exchange rates and interest rates, all of which can matter substantially in specific episodes. Fourth, exogenous shocks such as wars, pandemics, and sanctions were introduced through scenario assumptions rather than generated endogenously, so the model's usefulness depends on the analyst's ability to specify these shocks sensibly.

The findings also have implications for how uncertainty is treated. Because expectations drive prices, uncertainty about the future enters the model directly and not merely as noise around a deterministic path. Scenario simulation is a natural way to explore this, since it shows how different expectation paths lead to different price trajectories. Future work could extend this by running Monte Carlo experiments over uncertain parameters and shock timing, producing distributions of outcomes instead of single trajectories. Sensitivity analysis could identify which loops and parameters most influence price volatility, guiding both data collection and policy design.

Several extensions would strengthen the model. Disaggregating supply by producer type would allow the representation of different response speeds and strategic motives. Adding a financial sector with speculative demand and inventory-holding behavior could improve the representation of short-term volatility. Including substitution effects from renewable energy and the longer-run impact of climate policy would make the model more relevant for long-horizon analysis. Finally, expectations could be estimated from survey data or market-implied measures, such as futures curves, instead of being assumed, which would tie the central mechanism more closely to observation.

In conclusion, this paper has proposed a data-driven system dynamics model of the oil market in which price is determined by expected demand and supply relative to their actual values. The core of the model is built from regression analysis of historical time series and is refined with causal loops representing key feedback mechanisms in the market. Simulations of several past scenarios produced price trends consistent with those that actually occurred, supporting the argument that expectations and feedback delays are essential for explaining sharp price changes. While the model should be validated further through out-of-sample testing and extended to include more heterogeneous actors and financial factors, it offers a transparent and flexible framework for analyzing the oil market under uncertainty. It can serve both as a forecasting aid and as a tool for examining how shocks and changing expectations shape future price behavior.

Consumers rarely know every product available to them. Someone looking for a hotel, a book, or a streaming show typically starts with a handful of options that come to mind or appear on the first page of a platform. From there, the consumer faces two distinct choices. He can inspect an option he already knows about, learning its match value and price, or he can broaden his horizon and discover further products. Recommendation lists, "load more" buttons, filters, and the browsing of category pages are all instruments of this second activity. Discovery does not reveal the value of a product; it only makes the product available for later inspection. Search then resolves uncertainty about products the consumer already knows.

The existing literature largely separates these two activities. In the classical sequential search model of Weitzman (1979), the consumer knows the set of alternatives and the distribution of values of each one, and chooses the order in which to inspect them and when to stop. The optimal policy is elegantly simple: each alternative has a reservation value, the consumer inspects in descending order of these values, and stops when the best realized value exceeds all remaining reservation values. In random search models, in contrast, the consumer cannot direct his attention and simply samples the next product from a population. Neither framework captures a consumer who must decide, at each moment, whether to look more closely at what he has or to expand the set of things he could look at.

This paper studies exactly that problem. A consumer begins aware of a small set of products. At every point in time, he can either pay a search cost to inspect a known product, thereby uncovering its value, or pay a discovery cost to become aware of additional products. Discovered products are added to the pool of known alternatives, and they in turn can be inspected, bought, or ignored. The consumer's problem is thus a joint one: what to inspect, when to discover, and when to stop and purchase. The difficulty is that discovery generates an option whose value depends on the future search policy, which in turn depends on what discovery uncovers. A priori the problem is a dynamic program with a state space that grows with the set of known and inspected products.

My first contribution is to show that, despite this complexity, the optimal policy is fully characterized by tractable reservation values. Each known product has a reservation value, as in Weitzman's problem, that depends only on its own value distribution and search cost. Discovery is likewise assigned a reservation value, which captures the expected benefit of expanding the set of known products and the cost of doing so. The consumer compares these values with each other and with the best value realized so far. Because every quantity is computed separately for each action, the optimal policy can be described without solving the full dynamic program. The result extends the logic of index policies to settings in which actions change the set of available actions.

My second contribution concerns the purchase decision. I prove that a predetermined index fully specifies which product a consumer following the optimal policy ends up buying. The index is a function of the product's characteristics alone and is independent of the order in which products happen to be discovered or inspected. This property is useful for two reasons. It makes the choice of an optimal searcher easy to predict and to embed in empirical or equilibrium models, since one need only compare indices rather than track the path of search. It also clarifies what drives purchases: a product's index combines its value distribution, its search cost, and its position in the discovery process, so that a product that is hard to find can be less likely to be bought even when it would be valuable once inspected.

Third, I compare the optimal search and discovery policy with classical random and directed search. Under random search, the consumer has no control over which product he encounters, so discovery and inspection are bundled. Under directed search, the consumer chooses the order of inspection but takes the set of products as given. The comparison shows where the benchmarks fail. Models of directed search overstate the consumer's ability to find high-value products when awareness is limited, while random search understates his ability to steer toward promising alternatives once they are known. The optimal policy interleaves the two. A consumer may inspect a mediocre known product rather than discover, or may discover despite having unsearched alternatives, depending on how their reservation values compare. I highlight how the resulting purchase patterns, such as the probability of buying products that were known from the start, differ from either benchmark.

These results matter for the design of platforms and for the analysis of markets with limited consumer awareness. Platforms control both the initial set of products shown and the cost of discovering more, through ranking, pagination, and recommendations. Understanding how consumers trade off these margins is a prerequisite for evaluating such design choices and for modeling how firms compete to be known as well as to be chosen.

The paper relates to work on sequential search (Weitzman 1979; Armstrong 2017), consideration sets and limited awareness, and optimal stopping with expanding option sets. The remainder is organized as follows. Section 2 sets up the model. Section 3 derives the optimal policy. Section 4 establishes the index representation of purchases. Section 5 compares the policy with random and directed search, and Section 6 concludes.

We consider a single consumer who must eventually choose one product or take an outside option. The model is set in discrete decision epochs with a Pandora's-box structure extended by a discovery margin.

**Environment.** There is a countable set of products. At any time the consumer is aware of a subset, the *known set*, and unaware of the rest. Each known product i is characterized by a match value u_i, which is unknown until inspected. Before inspection the consumer knows only its distribution F_i, with finite mean. Inspecting product i costs s_i ≥ 0 and fully reveals u_i. Values are independent across products. The outside option has value u_0, known and constant. Recall is free: the consumer may choose any inspected product at no further cost, and the process ends when he stops and takes a product or the outside option.

**Discovery.** At any time the consumer may instead pay a cost d > 0 to discover a new product. Discovery draws a product from an unaware pool and adds it to the known set, without revealing its match value. Each discovered product has a type (F_i, s_i) drawn i.i.d. from a known distribution G over types, so the pool is statistically stationary. The consumer then faces the next decision with an enlarged known set. This formulation makes discovery itself a stochastic, repeatable action, whose value comes from the option of searching the product acquired.

**Decision problem.** The state consists of the best inspected value so far, y (initially u_0), the set of uninspected known products, and the discovery technology (d, G). In each period the consumer selects one of four actions: stop and take the best inspected option; inspect a known uninspected product; discover; or, trivially, a combination of these over time. He maximizes expected final payoff, which is the maximum of observed values, minus total search and discovery costs. We assume no discounting, so that the problem is stationary, and assume the stopping problem is well-posed through integrability of the u_i.
